utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-87-T, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's hearing and the subsequent hearings to complete the case are those during which we will hear closing arguments for all parties. Mr. Bakrac, we've been advised of the state of health of Mr. Lazarevic, who is recovering from treatment, I understand, and I see that he's not present in court this morning. I understand that he is content that these hearings should proceed in his absence. Can you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that. I was with him yesterday in the prison hospital, and he agreed that we continue the proceedings without his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac, for confirming that. We will now proceed to hear the closing arguments for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. For the record, I'm Tom Hannis on behalf of the Office of the Prosecution. I'm joined today by our case manager, Mr. Ian Reid, trial attorney Daniela Kravetz, and my co-senior trial attorney, Mr. Chester Stamp. It is an honour, Your Honours, to appear before you again this one last time. The weight of my responsibility to address remarks to you about the Prosecution's case weighs heavily upon me, but I feel confident that there is substantial evidence to support the arguments that we will be making. I guess in context to the time, Your Honours, I feel a little bit like I'm at the Olympic finals of trial advocacy. I hope I can at least make the finals, if not earn a medal. We're here to talk about the crimes that were committed in Kosovo in 1999. The Prosecution has said in our indictment and throughout this trial that these six accused were participants in a joint criminal enterprise, the purpose of which was to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to ensure continued Serb control over that province. And before I go on to speak about that, Your Honours, I should explain to you the order in which we intend to proceed. I'm going to make some introductory remarks in terms of an overview, talk a little bit about the background leading up to these crimes. Ms. Kravetz will follow me and speak briefly about the pattern of the crimes and the crime base and why people left Kosovo in the spring of 1999. She will be followed by Mr. Stamp who will talk about the bodies evidence that's been a big part of this case and about the individual responsibility of Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Lukic. Then you will hear from me a second time. I'll address the individual criminal responsibility of our military accused, General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, and General Lazarevic. And we will conclude with some general observations about the evidence and the approach that I would like to suggest that Your Honours follow in reviewing all the evidence that you've seen and heard in this case. Now, as I said, this joint criminal enterprise to alter the ethnic balance to help maintain Serb control in Kosovo was -- was to be achieved by criminal means, and in this case those criminal means took the form of a widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at the Kosovo Albanian population. Now, the man with a plan about carrying this out was Slobodan Milosevic. And one of the first and most, I guess, chilling examples of the fact that he had a plan and the nature of the plan is found during a 24 October 1998 meeting that Mr. Milosevic had with General Naumann and General Clark. You heard the evidence of General Naumann when he was here and he told us how during that meeting after the agreement had been signed, Mr. Milosevic became agitated and said that a final solution to the Kosovo problem would be found in the spring, and when Naumann and Clark pressed Mr. Milosevic for an explanation of what he -- what he meant by that exactly, he said, "We'll do what we did in Drenica in 1946." They weren't quite familiar what that was, they asked him to explain and he said, "We got them all together and shot them." And indeed in March through May 1999, you see examples of those kind of crimes of people being taken away and shot, of people being forced to leave their homes. These crimes in March through May 1999, we say, were the next logical step in a series of ever more oppressive measures to try to deal with the Kosovo problem, and these go back, Your Honour, 10 or 20 years before the crimes. Now, with regard to the participants in the joint criminal enterprise, let me show you the next slide. We have Mr. Milosevic, President Milutinovic. He was a part of the Supreme Defence Council which we say later came to be called the Supreme Command during the state of war, and the Supreme Command directed and controlled and made decisions about the use of the VJ, the army, during the conflict. Heading the VJ during that time was General Ojdanic as chief of the Supreme Command Staff as it was known during the wartime. Directly subordinate to him was General Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army. And his immediate subordinate commanding the Pristina Corps was General Lazarevic who was commander over the VJ brigades and later the Pristina military district was resubordinated to him. We say those forces were a substantial portion of the forces that helped carry out the crimes in Kosovo in 1999 during the war. Also in this joint criminal enterprise, we say, was Mr. Sainovic who played a significant role through his activities with the Joint Command, both in 1998, particularly during the time that the 1998 plan for the suppression of terrorism was carried out, and also we say in 1999. Helping complete the membership in the joint criminal enterprise, those participants who had an active role in engaging the forces that actually committed the crimes hands-on, General Lukic, head of the MUP staff in Kosovo. Now, I just want to address briefly the forces that were involved in the crimes. We have the Yugoslav army. And, Your Honour, for everyone who is watching, if you want to see the visuals that I'm referring to they're on the e-court channel as these slides come up. The Serb forces or the Yugoslav army, the VJ, both active and reserve in the Ministry of Interior. Police active and reserve. The military district, particularly the military territorial detachments, and others including what we've referred to in several instances as the armed non-Siptar population. We'll talk more about that later. Just -- I'd like to put up quickly one slide showing the command structure of the army. This is an attachment, I believe, to our final brief and an exhibit in the case. One more slide for you is a slide showing Kosovo and the general outlines and the areas of responsibility of the VJ brigades active in Kosovo in 1999. And the 125th under Colonel Zivanovic. The 549th under General Delic, 243rd under Colonel Jelic, the 15th Armoured Brigade under Colonel Gergar. The MUP. I'll put up the slide showing the structure and you'll see that General Lukic was head of the MUP staff and where they fit into the organisational structure. We have the military district, and we'll talk more later about their role. The others included Ministry of Defence units such as the Civil Defence and civil protection, local or village defence, armed non-Siptar population, the paramilitaries, and volunteers. Now, how were all these bodies engaged and how were they controlled and used to take part in these crimes? Well, in part through various coordination and control entities. First of all, we had the SDC, the Supreme Defence Council, and as it was known during wartime the Supreme Command. For the army we had the VJ General Staff prior to the commencement and the state of war and then became known as the Supreme Command staff during the state of war. For the MUP forces in Kosovo we had the MUP staff. And then there was another body that we talked about a lot in this case and we will talk about a lot during these closing remarks. That was the Joint Command, and I will address that in some detail when I return to speak later on at the end of the day or tomorrow. Now, the plan or common purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was to maintain Serb control of the province by altering the ethnic balance, and that occurred primarily by removing ethnic Albanians from Kosovo. This wasn't a plan that developed in an instant. We say this was something that developed over time, over a long period of time, after other efforts to deal with the Kosovo problem had proved unsuccessful. And in simple terms, the Kosovo problem was too many Albanians, too many Albanians with separatist intentions and the effect that had on the Serbs who lived in Kosovo. There's a lot more detail about this in our brief, Your Honours, I think beginning at paragraphs 28 to 83. I just want to highlight some of these key points. During the 1980s, one of the principal grievances of Serb nationalists circles was that the constitution of the SFRY gave Kosovo substantial autonomy, and as a result of that, Kosovo Serbs were vulnerable to discrimination by a government that was dominated by ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. By the early 1990s, we say the preservation of Serbian control in Kosovo had become central to Mr. Milosevic and Serbian policy. There were a number of legislative changes that began to occur in late 1998. In the spring of 1999, you've heard the evidence about special measures that were introduced in Kosovo. And in March of 1999, the Serbian Assembly proposed amendments to the Serbian constitution that would in effect strip Kosovo of most of its autonomy. And in late March 1989, Kosovo's autonomy indeed was effectively revoked. We have evidence that police repression against Kosovo Albanians increased dramatically after that point in time. We have evidence from Fred Abrahams, Veton Surroi, Adnan Merovci, and Ibrahim Rugova, among others, held during the 1990s most of the Kosovo Albanian language schools were closed. Most of the employees of ethnic Albanian nature were fired from the University of Pristina. Kosovo Albanians were dismissed from managerial and directorial positions. And yet in spite of that during that time period in the early 1990s, the Kosovo Albanians primarily pursued a policy of civil resistance and they did establish an unofficial parallel system of health care and education, but the problem persisted. The Serbian authorities made attempts to address the problem in Kosovo by bringing more Serbs into Kosovo, some of the Serb refugees from the conflicts elsewhere in Yugoslavia, but those efforts we say also did not prove to be very successful. The problem continued. On the Albanian side the -- the more outspoken critics of the Serb policy began to support violence as an alternate means to deal with the problem. Mr. Rugova and his policies lost favour with substantial numbers of those individuals, and the violence in Kosovo increased. We say this led to the formation of the Joint Command in 1998 in conjunction with the 1998 plan to suppress terrorism. And finally, when that also failed to adequately solve the problem, we say it led to the 1999 crimes under cover of the NATO conflict. Now, the Defence has argued throughout the trial and in their closing briefs that there was no plan, that there was no joint criminal enterprise. We say, Your Honour, and when we wrap up our arguments we will hope to have presented several details and examples to support our primary argument that the existence of the plan to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo by criminal means is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the totality of the evidence in this case. Now, the plan or common purpose doesn't have to be written down in a document or declared in a speech. I say since the end of World War II and Nazi Germany people who make a decision to engage in a programme like this are not going to put it down in writing and say this is our plan to expel Kosovo Albanians. You shouldn't expect to find such a document. Indeed if you did, you should be suspicious about it. So in essence, Your Honour, we have a circumstantial case and I will talk about circumstantial evidence when I come back to you later on to make my final remarks at the end. Part of the evidence that supports that statement I just made about the only reasonable conclusion to be drawn is from the pattern of the crimes that were committed, the deportations, the forcible transfers, the murders, and the persecutions. There's a pattern, too, in how these crimes were carried out in March, April, May of 1999. An illustration of that is found in part from looking at the Joint Command orders at the beginning of the war. On your screen you'll see now some examples from the Joint Command orders during the period between 23 March and 4 April 1999 showing the areas where combat actions were carried out, joint actions between the VJ and the MUP, and we'll talk later how those areas coincide with our crime sites and with the testimony of victim witnesses who were eyewitnesses to some of the killings and themselves suffered the deportations, and in some cases actually survived massacres of their fellow villagers. The next slide is another illustration of Joint Command orders for a later period, from mid to late April 1999, again showing areas that coincide with where we say crimes actually occurred. Your Honours, that's the conclusion of my overview. Now I'd like to turn the podium over to Ms. Kravetz who is going to talk about the crime base and the pattern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The question that has been asked over and over again in this courtroom during the course of the last two years is why did the Kosovo Albanian population flee in large numbers during the indictment period. Now, the Defence in this case do not contest the fact that there was a large scale departure of Kosovo Albanians during the period that we are concerned with in this case. The contested issues are the reasons for this departure. Now, the OTP's position is that the departure of over 800.000 Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo was mainly due to the actions of the forces of the FRY and Serbia, of the actions of the VJ and the police acting in a coordinated manner and under the command of the accused. These forces forced the population to flee the province. Now, we say the evidence presented in this case establishes beyond reasonable doubt that this was the main cause for departure, and I will be speaking about the reasons why we think this has been proven to you. Beginning on 24th March 1999, which we know is a date that NATO started bombing Kosovo and continuing on through April and May 1999, the forces of the FRY and Serbia acting in a concerted and coordinated manner launched a widespread and systematic attack on Kosovo Albanian villages throughout the province aimed at driving the Kosovo Albanian population out. The accused in this case used the NATO bombing as a window of opportunity to carry out the common plan. Mr. Hannis has just spoken about the common purpose of the JCE that is charged in this indictment. During these attacks that were carried out throughout the province, these forces systematically looted property belonging to Kosovo Albanians, massacred civilians, and we've heard evidence in this case of numerous instances of killings of civilians during this attack. They sexually assaulted Kosovo Albanian women, destroyed businesses, burned down shops and burned down homes of those being expelled in an effort to leave nothing behind for those who were expelled to return to. Now, typically we've heard this from the evidence, VJ forces would shell the villages to force the civilians to flee. Later MUP forces would enter on foot and conduct house-to-house searches and expel remaining civilians. The civilians would normally be channeled to transit areas from where they would be boarded on buses or trains or forced to take their own vehicles and directed to border crossing points. Sometimes they would be forced to walk for many hours, sometimes days to reach the border. And we heard in this case the testimony of many witnesses who told us about their plight in reaching these border crossings. These attacks that were carried out throughout the province created an atmosphere of terror. The residents of villages in one part of the municipality would flee upon hearing that attacks were being conducted in other villages or in neighbouring villages, neighbouring towns of their municipality. The Kosovo Albanian population had no choice but to flee their homes and -- in fear of these attacks. The evidence of the pattern that emerges from the testimony that we've heard in this case is compelling. On 24th March we hear that villages were attacked in municipalities across Kosovo, in Orahovac, Suva Reka, Kosovska Mitrovica, Vucitrn, Kacanik, Urosevac, simply to provide some examples. These attacks happened again and again and again. I will not go through every instance charged in the indictment, every example. We have submitted quite lengthy written submissions in this case and due to time constraints I'm not able to cover each one of them, but I would like to focus on one example and this is Pristina because we say it illustrates the pattern that was to follow of these attacks carried out throughout the province. Now, Pristina, as you know, was the capital of the province or is still the capital of the province. It was also the place where the accused met -- several of the accused had their headquarters during the relevant time. The Chamber will probably remember the testimony of several witnesses who spoke about events in Pristina, Emin Kabashi, Nazalie Bala, K62, K63, and these witnesses told us that the expulsions in this municipality of Kosovo Albanian residents began on and around 24th March and continued throughout the last week of March and into the first week of April. This is when the largest wave of expulsions was carried out. Now, these expulsions were carried out systematically with force and intimidation and we heard from witnesses how mixed groups of police, soldiers, and sometimes local Serbs who joined in these expulsions went from house to house forcing civilians to leave or face death. In many instances once the residents would leave their homes, their homes would be burnt down, their shops and businesses destroyed. We also heard testimony from a couple of protected witnesses that during these expulsions women were sexually assaulted in their homes by forces breaking into their homes to force residents to leave. Now, the residents of Pristina municipality were directed towards the centre of town, to the train station, where they were forced to board trains that would take them south to the Macedonian border. Your Honours, this was not a humanitarian evacuation or an evacuation conducted for any legitimate purpose. Your Honours probably remember in the testimony of Emin Kabashi who was one of the persons at the train station, and we have the slide up of an excerpt of his witness statement, who spent several days there trying to board a train and who spoke about the thousands of people that arrived to the train station in Pristina who were forced onto trains, and he said that he witnessed the police herding these people onto trains like cattle. And we heard the testimony of several witnesses who were on board these trains, Nazalie Bala, for example, who told us about the conditions aboard these trains, about how crowded they were. They had no windows. People could barely move. And K62, who was also at the train station, told us that she was afraid that she would die because there were so many people at that train station. These civilians were transported by train to the Macedonian border and as we've heard from several witnesses, including Mr. Bucaliu who worked at the Urosevac train station, during the last week of March and going into the first week of April the frequency of trains travel from Pristina through Orahovac and on to the Macedonian border was increased and so were the numbers of cars on the trains in order to be able to deport larger numbers of people out of the province. Now, these trains would go to the border crowded with people and would return empty, and at the border, police tore the IDs of the refugees and told them to cross over, that this was not -- this was Serbian territory, that they should go into Macedonia. This same pattern of expulsions that I've just very briefly gone over that we heard about in Pristina was repeated in municipalities across Kosovo. This repetition of the same type of events in different municipalities show that these attacks were not isolated acts. These were not coincidental events. These attacks were planned. They were organised, and the consequences were intended. They were aimed at forcing the civilian population out of the province. There are more examples that will be referred to later in this case -- later in our presentation by Mr. Hannis, so I will not go into more examples of our crime base, but I do want to address some of the Defence arguments that have been raised in this case and also in the Defence submissions that have been filed. Now, the Defence have advanced several different possible explanations as to why the population left. We've heard that the -- arguments in the sense that the population left because they were fleeing NATO bombing, the KLA was forcing them to flee because they were trying to create a humanitarian crisis. We've heard them argue that Serb forces were not really forcibly deporting the population but they were simply escorting them to the border to assist them and remove them from combat zones and protect the population. And we've also heard arguments in the sense that the population was fleeing because there was fighting going on, legitimate combat, between Serb forces and the KLA. We say that these reasons do not explain why the population left, and I will first turn to the argument of -- that the people or the population left because of NATO. Now, this has been asserted by the Defence as a kind of mantra in this case in the face of overwhelming evidence to the contrary that the Kosovo Albanian population mainly fled because they were fearing NATO bombing which in fact started, as I said, when these attacks began throughout the province. Now, numerous witnesses who lived through these events, who were in Kosovo at the time and survived these events, they were the lucky ones to survive the events, came to this courtroom and told you that this was not the reason why they fled from the province, and we have the slide of the testimony of Ms. Bala as just one example of the many witnesses who testified about this, who said that she and her family did not leave Pristina because of NATO bombing. She said, "We were forced to leave by the army, the police, and the other forces that were present in Pristina at the time." And Your Honours probably remember the numerous witnesses who testified about this and stated similar -- gave a similar response to that of Ms. Bala. General Smiljanic from the air force, commander of the Serb air force, testified in this case and we have the testimony up there on the screen, and he told us that one of the areas that was most heavily bombed by NATO during their campaign in Kosovo was precisely the border area between Albania and Macedonia. He said that 80 per cent of fire was opened in this area, and this was the area that was most heavily bombed or destroyed. Now, why would civilians, if they were fleeing because of the NATO bombing, head precisely to the areas where the bombs were falling? Why would they put themselves and their family members in harm's way and head to the areas that were being bombed? Now, that doesn't really make sense, Your Honours, does it? We also know that at the same time that Kosovo was being bombed by NATO, Belgrade was also being heavily bombed but we did not see the waves of refugees that we saw departing from Kosovo departing from Belgrade during these bombings. The fact is, Your Honours, that the evidence clearly shows that this was not the reason for the departure of the population. Now, turning to the argument that the departures were really humanitarian evacuations, that Serb forces were simply removing civilians from combat zones, we know that is not true from the testimony of witnesses who said that when they arrived to the border their identity cards were confiscated, their licence plates from their cars when they were travelling in cars were seized and torn up and the documents were torn up, and they were forced across the border. This practice that we have termed in our brief of identity cleansing was aimed precisely at forcing people out and preventing them from returning. This was not a humanitarian evacuation. Now, it is true that some civilians fled certain areas because there was fighting going on, and they heard that Serb forces were advancing in the direction of their villages and we have testimony to that effect. We should not forget, Your Honours, however, that only six months prior to this campaign that was launched in March 1999 and I'm speaking about the period of the summer offensive of -- conducted between August and October 1998, Serb forces in that period conducted a widespread campaign throughout the province during which thousands of civilians were internally displaced. Kosovo Albanian villages were burned. Some were razed to the ground. Of course civilians would flee in March and April upon hearing that Serb forces were heading their way. They had lived through similar events only six or seven months prior. They had suffered the consequences of these attacks. They knew the fate that awaited them if they remained in their villages and they feared for their lives. They had no choice but to flee from their homes and from their villages. I want to turn now to some of the murder incidents that are charged in the indictment and I will only go very briefly through some of the Defence arguments that had been raised regarding some of our killing sites. Now, the Defence have argued with respect to the murders that Serb forces were really conduct -- simply conducting a legitimate campaign, anti-terrorist actions against the KLA, and that the victims of these murder incidents were either victims caught in the crossfire or legitimate combatants, members of the KLA that were legitimately killed during these anti-terrorist operations. Your Honours, there was no KLA presence at 157 Milos Gilic Street in Djakovica in early April when police forces attacked this house. There were only 20 civilians, mostly -- 19 of them were women and children who had hid in the basement seeking shelter and they were forced out of the basement by the police and shot dead and Your Honours heard that -- the harrowing account of Dren Caka who was the sole survivor. He was only 10 years old at the time and he witnessed his mother and sister being shot and he told us he survived only because he pretended to be dead and then he escaped out a window and we know that this house was later burnt down by the Serb police. There was also no KLA presence and no fighting going on at the pizzeria in Suva Reka where three branches of the Berisha family gathered and they were forced there by, again, Serb police. Around 40 -- over 40 people were shot dead, all members of the Berisha family, a large number of them were women and children, by Serb police and later explosives were thrown in the pizzeria. And we know from the evidence, from forensic evidence that the bodies of these persons were at first buried outside in Prizren in a firing range and they were later transported outside of Belgrade and buried in clandestine mass graves. Now, one wonders if these were really legitimate killings, why someone would go through the trouble of transporting bodies over 280 kilometres from Suva Reka and hiding them in mass graves. Clearly these were not legitimate killings. These were civilians who were specifically targeted because they were Kosovo Albanians. Turning to Izbica, we've heard evidence to the effect that there was fighting going on and that these persons killed were probably members of the KLA. Now, Your Honours saw the images that were filmed by Dr. Liri Loshi who arrived to Izbica only days after the massacre had occurred and it is clear from the images that the victims of this massacre were mostly elderly men. We heard testimony one of them was handicapped. There were also two women who were burned on a tractor. They were burned alive by Serb forces and these were persons who had gathered along with thousands of others who had been expelled from their homes in other villages of the municipality. They had gathered in a meadow hoping that by staying there in the open Serb forces would not attack them and that they would be protected and they even had white sheets to show that they were not fighting. And these persons were shot dead and as we know later, their bodies were also found in a mass grave, some of the bodies of these victims were also found in a mass grave in Petrovo Selo in Serbia proper. And the last incident -- murder incident that I want to refer to is Kotlina which we've heard extensive evidence about in this case as well. We know from the testimony of an eyewitness to this event that Serbian police and soldiers captured a group of men who had fled and hidden in -- up a hill in the forest, and they beat these men and took them to some -- two water wells that -- water holes that had been dug outside the village. These persons were shot dead and then their bodies were thrown down the well shaft and explosives were thrown down. The circumstances of these killings shows that this was not a legitimate killing. These were not persons that were engaged in any type of fighting, and the forensic evidence which has been tendered in this case proves that -- corroborates the testimony that these persons died from gunshot wounds and from the effects of the explosives. Their bodies were actually dug out of the well. That's where forensics found them. Another argument that has been advanced regarding the murders is that these murders were committed for personal motives, that the persons were not acting in an official capacity, they were not acting under orders of the police or the VJ. We know from the evidence that these murders usually occurred when the villages were being -- were attacked, that when they were being cleansed as is -- as is the term referred to often in some of the documents that are cited in the brief, the military documents, there was a similar pattern in these crimes, these murders, that shows that these were part of a campaign and that they were aimed at terrorising civilians. They were aimed at forcing others to flee. And in many occasions the victims were men, and they were simply killed because they were able-bodied men who were captured in, like the examples that I have given, and simply killed in cold blood. Many of the victims were also women and children, and these were murders, as I said, that happened during the attacks on the villages when the populations were being forced to flee. Now, we have charged in this case a count of persecution which includes the deportations and murders that I have already spoken about. It also includes allegations of sexual assault which we say also forms part of this campaign aimed at terrorising civilians and intended to force civilians to flee the province, and we have presented before Your Honours several examples of how these murders occurred. You have heard the testimony of several protected witnesses. I'm not going to recite that here. It is in the brief. And these attacks also -- these sexual assaults also occurred during the course of the expulsions, and I've given the example of Pristina where we heard the testimony of one protected witness who was assaulted in her home when Serb forces broke in to expel the residents. We have also charged as part of our count of persecution the destruction of religious sites. It's another type of crime that's charged under persecution. These acts were not only criminal but the fact that religious institutions, mostly mosques, from what we heard in the evidence were destroyed reflects the intent that I referred to earlier of leaving nothing behind for these expelled to come back to. The evidence that has been presented in this case refutes the suggestion of the Defence that this destruction occurred because of the NATO bombing. We know from the testimony of several witnesses that many of these mosques were destroyed on and around the same date, 28th March, which was not a date that was chosen by coincidence. As you know, this was the date of an important Muslim holiday, Bajram, and in several municipalities we saw that the mosques were destroyed on this date. Now, an issue that has been raised by the Defence with regard to all the crimes is the issue of perpetrator ID. Who were the actual perpetrators of these crimes? Mr. Hannis has already described to you the forces that we allege were on the ground at the time. This is already explained in quite some detail in our brief. Our position is that MUP and VJ forces were the only significant forces that were deployed in Kosovo at the time and that any other armed -- organised armed group that was operating there was operating under the command and control of VJ and MUP forces, and in our brief we have cited numerous examples for each crime site, of military orders showing the units that were deployed there. And we also heard from several insider witnesses who told us where there -- where they were deployed and where they conducted actions. There -- there were simply, Your Honours, no other significant forces on the ground other than the Serb forces. And we do have to keep in mind that Kosovo is a very small territory. I don't know if you remember our opening where we showed you Kosovo superimposed on a map of Holland and Belgium to show you the dimensions of how small a territory we're talking about and it is our position that Serbian forces, the VJ and MUP controlled the areas of responsibilities where they were operating. So there were no rogue elements operating in these municipalities that we were -- have charged. These units were participating together with VJ and MUP forces to carry out the common plan that has been charged in this case. Now we'll turn very briefly to some legal submissions. Our legal submissions on the elements of the crimes that have been charged are contained in our pre-trial brief. These are paragraphs 6 to 40 of our pre-trial brief where we refer to the legal elements of war crimes and crimes against humanity and the specific counts charged. I'm not going to repeat that here and these submissions were not reiterated in our closing briefs so I refer Your Honours to our pre-trial brief with that respect. Mr. Hannis has referred to the common purpose of the JCE, and now with respect to the crimes charged, we say that counts 1 and 2, that is the crime of deportation and forcible transfer, form the core of the common purpose as charged in the indictment. With respect to the remaining counts that is count 3 and 4, murder as a crime against humanity and war crimes and persecutions, it is our position that these crimes were either part of the common purpose and were intended by the members of the JCE including the accused or that they were natural and foreseeable consequences of the common purpose and the accused nevertheless took the risk and implemented this plan. Now, during the course of this case Your Honours have probably asked yourselves why the crimes that we've heard about in this case occurred, especially when listening to some of the survivors of these horrible events that took place in Kosovo. These crimes occurred because the political leadership, the leadership of the police and the VJ caused these crimes to occur. The accused in this case caused these crimes to happen in Kosovo, Your Honours. I will now yield the floor to Mr. Stamp, who will continue with the submissions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, I wonder if you could clarify for me your submission at the beginning about the common plan. Your submission is that this plan existed from at the latest October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We have charged in the indictment that the common --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but is that your submission as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My submission is that the pattern of attacks that we saw in Kosovo began -- and this is because the indictment has, of course, been restricted and the Racak incident has been dropped. So I'm not speaking about events in January; I'm just speaking about events that started once the NATO bomb began. So our submission is that the campaign of attacks that we saw in Kosovo began on 24th March 1999. We have addressed in our brief what happened in the months prior to that, the build-up of forces before this campaign was launched. And as Mr. Hannis has pointed out and I have also pointed out in my submissions, it is our position that the accused used the cover of the NATO bombing which was started -- began on 24th March to implement the common plan, but there was a build-up, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's that I want to ask you about and I don't think it's an answer to say that the indictment has been restricted in some way. I mean, your case must reflect what you consider the evidence demonstrates, and what I'd like to be clear about is whether you're saying that even prior to the negotiations at Rambouillet and Paris this plan existed. Is that your submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. It is our submission that the JCE came into effect at least in October 1998. The plan existed. My submission when I started this morning was that it was implemented, and I'm just referring to the crimes we have charged in the indictment, it was implemented or put into effect as of 24th March 1999. There was, of course, a build-up during that -- the months prior to the NATO bombing and -- which will be addressed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way you've put it though was that the -- and you've put it twice now this way, that authorities used the NATO bombing campaign as a cover for implementing the plan. Now, are you saying that that's something which just happened because of a developing set of circumstances, or are you saying that they went to the peace negotiations with the plan in mind that, "Well, when these break down, NATO will bomb us and we'll use that as a cover for removing the population"? And you see that would then lead me to ask you the question did they seriously think they could defeat NATO and also clear the country of Albanians? Is that your submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, I should say that the peace negotiations and the breakdown of the negotiations is a topic that Mr. Stamp will be addressing at quite some length in a bit. It is our submission that Serb -- Serb authorities went to these peace negotiations without a legitimate intention to reach a peaceful solution in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't mean to lead you into an area that you're not going to deal with and I'm happy to confine the questions to -- to what you're specifically dealing with at the moment. If I can go back to the earlier part of that question which became a compound question. Are you saying that it was -- the plan ended up being implemented in March because of a developing set of circumstances or because that was always the intention?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It is our position that that was always the intention, to carry out this campaign. And -- this is as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But how does it come to be related to the bombing campaign? That's what I'm trying to understand. Are you suggesting it was always envisaged that NATO would attack and that would be the ideal opportunity to remove the population, or are you saying there's a coincidence between these two?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that there is a coincidence. We have addressed in our brief the fact that already in the months prior to the NATO campaign there was planning going on between the VJ and the MUP and we speak specifically about a 17th February meeting which happened in the MUP and there are also orders coming down from the VJ which show that they had a clear intention to launch a campaign in Kosovo, and this was something that was not finished in October. They were stopped in October when they were launching this widespread campaign that I had spoken about earlier, and we all know what happened in October. The October agreements were signed and international forces came to the ground. But there was always the intention to carry out this campaign and to expel the population, and there was a build-up of forces which we speak about and we will speak about later also in some detail. Forces remained despite the agreements reached. Forces remained on the ground. And in February we discussed in our brief the fact that the MUP was planning these operations, and there's a statement which I don't have before me right now from Minister Stojiljkovic and also from Lukic who -- who say once the NATO bombing began that they planned to carry out operations in Kosovo. And unfortunately, I don't have the reference in front of me, but I do refer Your Honours to our brief where we are discussing this 17th February meeting, which is we say quite important and significant and shows the intention of authorities to conduct an offensive. This is discussed, Your Honours, in the section on the MUP staff where we're speaking about coordination between VJ and MUP -- MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting us, Ms. Kravetz. We can now proceed to hear Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours. The paragraphs I was referring to of our final trial brief are paragraphs 237 and 238, and I just refer Your Honours to those paragraphs. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As it is coming close to the end, may I also express my gratitude of being allowed to appear before this panel and to address this panel. I do not intend to be as speedy as a man by the name of Usain Bolt, as -- and the Jamaican woman at the Olympics as some of my learned colleagues on the other side have asked me to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Are you congratulating Judge Nosworthy on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think she probably takes pride in that she -- there is some connection to her as well. I think, Your Honours, that the Prosecution's closing brief is a very comprehensive document, and it covers the relevant evidence in the case very carefully. To some extent it has predicted some of the arguments of the Defence in their briefs, which is natural because many of the arguments and the issues were refined and developed and became obvious as the case progressed. My Lord Bonomy did ask a couple questions just now and I will respectfully ask if both myself and Mr. Hannis would be allowed to respond to you when we come to that part of the address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's perfectly acceptable, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to start by discussing a little bit further what Ms. Kravetz talked about, and that is the evidence from the crime base that there was a pattern, that the crimes committed were widespread and systematic, because Kosovo, notwithstanding that it is a relatively small place, is a place where occurred massive crimes. Hundreds of thousands of people were expelled, thousands were killed, and occurred in a pretty short period of time. And the scale and gravity of crimes that are discussed in the Prosecution's closing brief and just now by Ms. Kravetz are matters which impact on every aspect of this case, from the knowledge of the accused to the intention of the accused and to what the accused did and ought to have done. This, it is submitted, is not a situation where there might have been a few victims and, therefore, persons may say that well, there were rogue elements or there was nothing I could have done. This was, it is submitted, a massive organised criminal enterprise. So the Defence argument that the evidence shows nothing more than sporadic or random violence against Kosovo Albanians is not supported by the evidence. This argument is made primarily, I think, by Mr. Ojdanic at paragraph 18 of his closing brief where he says that the killings and incidents of expulsion were the result of individuals or small groups acting out of revenge or hatred or on the orders of local leaders. This is an attempt to minimise and localise the types of crimes we're talking about. Mr. Milutinovic, another example at paragraph 303 of his closing brief, submitted at the last bullet point of page 145, of his page 165, that it cannot reasonably be inferred from the crime base evidence that a criminal plan existed. The pattern from the crime base evidence, it is submitted, is obvious. Typical assaults on villages or population centres of Kosovo Albanians where the population are expelled and sometimes some parts of the forced population, mostly men, are separated and killed. And it is submitted and I join Ms. Kravetz in this submission, that that evidence considered in its entirety by itself is sufficient to show that there was a widespread and systematic campaign. However, the crime base evidence, that is the evidence of the victims, is augmented by the evidence of the clandestine transportation and concealment of the bodies of over 800 Kosovar Albanians into Serbia proper, and these bodies were discovered in 2001. This is largely unchallenged evidence that this occurred, but it is the submission of the Prosecution that the -- this Trial Chamber is entitled to draw many inferences or certain inferences from this unchallenged evidence. Some of them are pretty obvious, and one is that the mortal remains of these victims, of these persons, were the remains of persons who were victims of murder, and the parties who organised this trans-shipment and concealment were aware that these were murder victims, not combatants but murder victims, and were conscious of their guilt or their participation in these murders. Otherwise, the bodies, of course, I think it's pretty obvious, would not have been concealed and so much effort would not have been made to ship them. They would have been processed in the normal course of events. And -- well, before going on, I have a note here to make a correction. At paragraph 289 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, reference is made to a chart of -- at Annex C, and it says that it summarises evidence relating to the exhumation of bodies in Serbia. In fact, the proof of death chart in Annex C only summarises evidence in respect to victims from the murder sites listed in the schedules. It does not cover all of the bodies of the persons exhumed in Serbia, just the scheduled victims. And this is a chart that was filed by the Prosecution. It's the same chart filed on the 27th of July, 2007, in order to assist the Chamber in locating the forensic and other evidence relevant to the deceased persons who are related to each scheduled murder site in the indictment. And it includes the forensic evidence in respect to the examination of those human remains and also the identification evidence, DNA evidence, and to some degree the evidence of witnesses to the killings of these persons. And the evidence revealed as Dr. Baraybar testified, that the vast majority of the scheduled murder victims or the scheduled victims whose remains were recovered in Serbia in a state that enabled them to perform forensic examination, died from gunshot wounds that were inflicted it could be scientifically established on persons who were not engaged in combat. Another inference I think the Court is entitled to draw from the bodies evidence, if I may call it that, is the fact that these human remains were from different crimes committed at different places at different times. Many of them were first buried at different places, at different times, to be systematically disinterred, gathered and collected and then transported hundreds of miles to two places where they are buried in mass graves together proves, it is submitted, that these were not random killings where they were trying to conceal the evidence, but there was a widespread and organised campaign to conduct the killings. The parties, Your Honours, who organised the exercise to transfer these bodies -- well, not just the transfer, to collect them from so many places and then transfer them to Serbia must have -- these persons who organised it must have had knowledge and participation in the original murders. Otherwise, they would not have known, or they would not have been able to gather these bodies from these disparate places with such facility. The proof of death chart at Annex C, as I said, summarises the evidence in respect of the victims from the murder sites listed in the schedules to the indictment. There are many other Kosovo Albanian victims of murder during the indictment period whose remains were identified among those found in Serbia and who were not included on that chart because they were not linked to the scheduled murders. They along with the schedule victims whose remains were located in Serbia in 2001 are included in Exhibit P2798 which is a CD containing the consolidated list of persons reported missing in Kosovo and the status of the case as of October 2006 and this was supplied to the ICTY by the United Nations Mission in Kosovo and the UN Office of Missing Persons and Forensics. More unchallenged evidence. And on your screen you will see the CD. If you look at the various columns, you'll see column B is described as "State" in which the remains are returned or whether or not the case was closed and the remains were returned to the family. I think Mr. Baraybar testified about this. If we could scroll to the right you will see in column I the date of the event of the disappearance as reported. Your Honours -- well, I will come to this later, and in columns J and K respectfully, the location of the event of death or disappearance as reported and the municipality. And if you look in column O, that refers to the mass grave sites where these persons were later discovered in 2001. The entire exhibit covers well over 5.000 persons who were reported to the UN Office for Missing Persons. However, it is really the 600 plus whose bodies were located in Serbia that I am focused on, and I wish to make it clear that I do not say that the 5.000 plus bodies -- or persons that the exhibit refers to are necessarily relevant to this case. These were just all of the persons that the Office for Missing Persons recorded as missing. So the technology allows us and what you have before you, Your Honours, is a part of this exhibit. The technology in which the exhibit was presented allows us to sort it, and basically what Mr. Reid has done here is to sort the exhibit, to show only those victims whose bodies or whose remains were identified among those found in the mass graves in Serbia in Petrovo Selo and in Batajnica as shown in column O. And if you -- you can also sort the spreadsheet to show where these victims were killed or where they were reported as presumed killed, and that can be done by the click of a button, and it has been done. And if you look in column L, the village, and you scroll down, you will see from Bogicevii, in Pec, Brestovac, Orahovac, Cirez, Decani, Djakovica, Dobro Selo in Obilic, many of those bodies were found in Batajnica. One can see people from Glogovac found at Petrovo Selo, Decani, Izbica. In the municipality of Srbica, many of those were found at Batajnica, it can be seen. Many from Korenica. We heard a lot of evidence in respect to both Korenica and Izbica. Some were found at Batajnica, some at Petrovo Selo. Perhaps you could go a little faster. Meja. Well, there will be many from Meja. At least 300 bodies or -- or 300 persons were identified who were reported missing from Meja. And the -- they were reported missing -- if we could -- if we could -- well, it's -- there -- they were reported missing or presumed missing on the 27th of April. The Prosecution did lead evidence in respect to the Meja incident of the huge offensive by force of the FRY and Serbia which resulted in the killing of over 300 persons. Their bodies later to be found in Batajnica. If we scroll down. Here we can see here people from Pec. More from villages of Ramoc. We heard evidence about Ramoc, in Djakovica, Slovinje, in Lipljan or -- please forgive my translation. I show that to show -- to indicate to the Court that this wasn't a situation where maybe two incidents or a few incidents and somebody gathered some bodies and tried to hide them. This is a huge enterprise. And if you look at the dates when these people were killed, apart from the dates which are consistent with the Prosecution -- with the incidents in the schedules, for example, you'll see that the Meja victims were killed on the 27th of April as charged in the indictment. You'll see that there is a huge spread through the indictment, mostly March and April. I should advise the Court that there was one reported according to -- to the staff in January, I think, of 1999 and one in July, but I take it Your Honours would understand that in statistics of this nature the occasional error will creep in. We're talking about thousands of victims and that does not affect the overall result. I asked Mr. Reid to put on a map of Kosovo where these persons would have been killed, and the small dots indicate either single persons or small amounts of persons. The bigger dots indicates 15 or so. The very large ones, like the one to the south-west corner of the map, I think that is Meja, south, and that is where the -- a huge amount of these 600 victims were found. I think if you look to the centre of the map somewhere to the south in Suva Reka, you will see just a small dot. I should point out that the victims of Suva Reka were not included in the UN list of missing persons. I -- these persons were the original and first persons who were disinterred in Serbia and whose bodies were identified by the laboratory in Spain. Dr. Alonso, I think, testified about that. So if those had been included there would be another big green circle in the middle of Suva Reka. So I would submit, Your Honour, that analysis of this evidence disposes of the argument that there was not a massive organised killing campaign, and this is just the tip of the iceberg. And of course, a campaign so large involved high level organisation that is the only inference, it is my submission, and it is also supported by the evidence of those involved that persons, senior persons in the Ministry of Interior were involved in ordering some of these drivers to relocate the bodies. K88 of the MUP said that in Batajnica over a period of 20 days from early April 1999, there were at least six deliveries in large refrigerated trailers of these bodies. So it is submitted that the -- this organised campaign of killing was not done as isolated acts, but as Ms. Kravetz submitted, when we look at the killings especially where they are bunched, we see that they occurred in the course of massive deportations. So there is a question as to whether or not there was just a campaign of killings or of persecution, or whether these killings, which are obviously organised, obviously systematic, were also related to the deportations. And the Prosecution submits that the answer to that question is yes. If we -- the Meja evidence is probably the most striking evidence, and it is important evidence because that was an operation from the VJ side, was according to the evidence led by the Accused Lazarevic, although the evidence is that the murders were primarily committed by policemen. VJ and MUP forces came down the valley on the 27th of April, and this -- I'm referring to the evidence of Pnishi -- forgive the pronunciation, Dedaj and Peraj. MUP forces came down the valley, forced the population out at certain check-points. Men were separated and murdered in large quantities. And these men disappeared, the bodies disappeared. They were reported missing, presumed dead. Similarly Suva Reka, Izbica. The murders occurred where the population were being pushed out of those areas. Those bodies were found at Izbica -- sorry, at Petrovo Selo and Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, it may be something to do with the preparation of the transcript, I'm not sure, but going back to Meja, what is it you're actually saying about who was responsible for that? You say it was an operation for which the VJ were responsible. Then you say the murders were principally committed by policemen. And then you say MUP forces came down the valley and that the people were -- people were separated out and murdered. Can you help us on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. The evidence of Pnishi, Dedaj and Peraj is that as the force of the FRY and Serbia came down, people were killed by both VJ, by both soldiers, and by MUP. I -- I recall Pnishi's evidence on that in particular. It does appear from the evidence that the -- many of the murders were committed at MUP check-points, and that is the evidence of Peraj, Nike Peraj, who observed at two or three check-points dozens of men murdered. So I just said really as an aside that most appeared to have been killed at these check-points based on this evidence and the evidence is that as the forces came down, forces from both sides were involved in these killings. I could perhaps later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The crime base evidence is also supported by evidence, if I may move on, Your Honours, evidence of statistical demography, evidence from that field, and the evidence -- this evidence provides further confirmation that the allegations of killings were, A, linked to expulsions, and B, were widespread and systematic. Your Honours, I say that this evidence by itself is not of much use. It is merely confirmatory evidence. It confirms the crime base evidence. The evidence of Dr. Ball is consistent, as it turns out, with the crime base evidence, and is consistent with what I referred to as the bodies evidence. Dr. Ball's evidence is that the killing and migration patterns were not the result of random acts of violence by government forces or by any forces. He said that both the migration flows and the killing took place in well-defined peaks during roughly the same periods and in the same places indicating that they both resulted from a common cause. The observed patterns were not consistent with periods of NATO bombing and KLA activity but is consistent with the hypothesis that Yugoslavian forces conducted a campaign of killings and expulsions. So he says consistent with. He says that is -- the analysis does not prove that these offences were committed by Yugoslav forces. What proves it is evidence of the witnesses. Now, the -- this evidence was led by the Prosecution with the intention to assist the Chamber on specific issues of a highly technical nature where specialised scientific knowledge is required. It is not an area that one can -- well, the ordinary person can master very quickly. Statistical demography especially is applied to complex humanitarian situations, requires a person with requisite experience, knowledge, and skill in order to posit opinions to a trier of fact to help them to draw conclusions and to understand and determine the issues in dispute. The Ball report and its addenda are the work of Dr. Ball and other experts described, genuine experts in the field of statistics, demographics and application to a complex humanitarian crisis. The -- and that is apparent from the curriculum vitae provided. The basis of the attack on the work of Dr. Ball is on the basis of the report of Dr. Fruits who also testified in this case, and this is found mainly in the submissions of General Ojdanic from paragraph 126. Dr. Fruits, Your Honour, is not qualified in the field of statistical demographics and its application to humanitarian crises. He admitted that he has published only one article in the field of demographics, and it was an article that used demographic information to estimate government spending, and it's at 25978 of the transcript. Nor is he an expert in statistics, even though some of his work in urban planning and econometrics touch upon statistics. Fritz Scheuren who participated in writing the statistical part of the Ball report and a past president of the American Statistical Association, is an expert in statistics and Dr. Fruits wasn't even aware of that. Dr. Fruits in his evidence, when asked, he accepted that he's only familiar with the basics of the methodology that Dr. Ball and others used to estimate the number of deaths. That is what is called multiple systems estimation or capture recapture statistical procedure which has been used and is being used the world over to estimate the number of victims of diseases, wars, famines, et cetera. This is at 25980 where Dr. Fruits says that he was only familiar with the basics. Dr. Fruits from his cross-examination even displayed ignorance or lack of awareness of some of the basic terminology used the field, which can be seen from the exchange now on the screen. And asked about basic terminologies used in the study, he didn't know what it meant. And asked about his expertise in the field of applying statistics to demographic issues involving complex humanitarian crises he said, "I would consider himself an expert now. I've spent two years doing this." Your Honours, this according to his testimony, is a period of time that he spent preparing his report and for his testimony in this case. His expertise is really limited to his efforts on behalf of the Defence in this case. What is even more striking, and I make this submission very strongly because this is one of the really very technical areas of expertise that the Court had considered and to some extent a Court has to rely, it is submitted, upon the opinions of the expert because the material is not very -- very easy for a layman to master, what is significant is that Dr. Fruits in his report at section 11.2 states that "statistical analysis could have provided an objective and verifiable test of Dr. Ball's hypothesis." So this could have been tested by the application of statistical procedures. He admitted that over the two-year period that he had been working, and if we could see the text from 26024, he admitted that over the two-year period that he had been working on this case he had received the data sets that Dr. Ball used for his analysis and that's at 25999 of the transcript, so he had available to him the material that he could have applied statistical analysis to to test Dr. Ball's hypotheses. However, he did not perform this test. He had the means to test them scientifically, to document them and present them, but he did not. He did not even specify any of the procedures he said were available that could have been used to test Dr. Ball's methodology even though he admitted that it would have taken him one week out of the two years to do so, as is discernible from the extract of the transcript on the screen. He was a little bit flippant in the last answer. He said, "It would still probably take at least a week. I'm a bit more careful than other statisticians, I guess." The point really is that this is, it is submitted, a serious failure of an expert in seeking to criticise, apart from any of the terms that he used which were unwarranted, is my submission, but this is a serious failure for an expert to attempt to criticise and undermine the work of another expert in a field of this nature, to say he could have done scientific work on it but failed to do it and to present it before the trier of fact. Dr. Fruits offers very, very little more than a layman's critique of the expert evidence of Dr. Ball et al. in a very complex and highly technical field. So the crime base evidence and the witnesses discussed in the pre-trial -- in the closing brief and by Ms. Kravetz is consistent with Dr. Ball's findings, and this almost by reverse analysis to some degree confirms his methodology, although the purpose of his testimony is to see whether or not scientific analysis would confirm the evidence of the witnesses, which it did. Dr. Ball's expertise merely corroborates the overall picture that the killings and the expulsions coincided and that the NATO bombings and the actions of the KLA were not significant causes of the migrations. The questions, Your Honour, as to whether or not there was a massive campaign, whether or not it was organised, that is, systematic, I think from all the evidence should be answered yes. Whether the accused are party to it, it is submitted, also should be answered yes, and that -- may I inquire what time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, this would be a convenient time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I intend to move on when we resume. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will have a break now for half an hour and resume again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The essence of the Milutinovic Defence as disclosed from the evidence led by the Defence and from the argument in the closing brief is that he is not individually criminally responsible as he did nothing to contribute to any crimes, and insofar as they were crimes committed, he did nothing because he had limited or no authority to do anything, and in any case, the media reports that he received about the crimes contradicted or were contradicted by official reports that he was -- that he had. Thus, basically it is being said that he knew nothing and could do nothing even if he knew. The -- his powers and authorities have been discussed in the pre-trial brief, and part of the discussion is the submission by the Prosecution that the implementation of a JCE of this scale required not only that high-level participants take positive steps to implement it, as would the commanders of armies and other forces involved in the crimes, but also that they refrain from acting to impede it even if it was their duty to do so. And one of the questions for the Trial Chamber is this: If the Trial Chamber accepts that there was, in fact, a massive widespread, well-organised and systematic campaign of violence, including murders and arson and expulsions against the Kosovo Albanians as alleged in the indictment with thousands of killings and hundreds of thousands of expulsions over a three-month period, did Mr. Milutinovic as president of the country have a duty to act to protect the safety of the endangered population, and did he do what was required to discharge that duty? Does international law hold him to a standard in the particular circumstances of this case? The relevant law on the matter has been discussed in earlier litigation in this case and is further set out at paragraphs 602 and thereafter in the Prosecution's brief. One of the critical elements of this analysis is a question of notice and awareness. He must know about what is going on or have reasonable cause to believe that an investigation ought to be conducted into the allegations of these widespread crimes. It seems that the Milutinovic closing brief at paragraph 266 accepts that he did receive notice of crimes, including notice of their scale and gravity from the international media, but it goes on to say that this was contradicted by reports that he received from official sources, and there was no reason for him to disbelieve the competent structures authorised to conduct the war effort, and that is how the issue is disposed of. Well, firstly it is the Prosecution's submission that if the president of a country have a regard to the standards of international law as it has developed receives even from the media, through international media, allegations of ethnic cleansing in his country, then they cannot ignore it simply because he receives official reports that contradict it. It is submitted that the reports that he received in the media is sufficient evidence of notice that imposed on him a duty to do, as is indicated in the Prosecution's closing brief, as was said in the Simic case, everything that was possible for him to do with his powers to stop and to prevent these massive crimes. He had the duty and the ability to request from the MUP that they report to him as to what was happening in the country, and Mr. Markovic agreed that this was a means available to him whereby he could exert public pressure on the government. There is, however, a great deal of other convincing evidence that Mr. Milutinovic became aware of the crimes or became aware of credible allegations of them both in 1998 and 1999. That again is covered in the pre-trial brief, but of paramount importance which I'd like to highlight is evidence of Dr. Rugova and Mr. Merovci that Mr. Milutinovic was specifically told in early April of the crimes that Kosovo is being emptied of its Kosovo Albanian population in the course of a campaign of violence. He later on received the indictment in this case. Therefore, did he act to discharge his duty, or did he act in a manner which fulfilled the implementation of a joint criminal enterprise? The Defence of Mr. Milutinovic has throughout the case attempted to marginalise and minimalise -- marginalise him from the political process and to minimise his power and authority as president, and in the course of the case this was rested primarily on the fact and expert evidence of Ratko Markovic who is described in the closing brief of the Defence as an independent witness. Your Honours, it is submitted that he is no such thing. He is far from someone who could be described as an independent expert and is someone whose evidence, especially insofar as he seeks to minimise the role and the power of Mr. Milutinovic should be examined with extreme suspicion and caution. It should be recalled that Mr. Markovic had close connections with some of the members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, and he was intimately involved in some of the crucial events relating to the indictment in this case. He was a member of the government, many of whose members bear responsibility for the crimes committed by the force of the FRY in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that an accurate statement, Mr. Stamp? I thought he wasn't a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he was not a member of the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just like the Queen in a country or the president may not be a member of the government. Are you saying he had a government position? Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying he was a member of the government in the sense of the government that is a part -- or that comes out of the legislator or comes out of elected officials. Sometimes the term "government" - and I apologise if I use it loosely - covers the judiciary, the executive, and the -- the presidential aspects of a government and I was using the term "government" in that sense. However, I do not say that he was a member of what we sometimes term to be the executive government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've perhaps misunderstood. It's my mistake. Page 43, line 19. That is a reference to Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Markovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I heard that as Milutinovic. It's my mistake, I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Markovic is a member of the executive government. Mr. Milutinovic is not. So I was suggesting that his personal involvement in many of the pertinent issues make his opinion -- opinions unreliable to the extent that he has a personal interest in those opinions. He was also a member of the ruling political party, the SPS, and sat on its Executive Board. He was a deputy of the federal parliament, and from 1994 to 2000 he served as one of the five deputy prime ministers for the Republic of Serbia. He was personally engaged in negotiations in 1999 -- 1998 as a member of the FRY delegation and also in 1999 at Paris and Rambouillet, and he was a member of the constitutional commission that drafted some of the legislation. The fact that some of the documents that he drafted or had to draft are controversial documents in this case makes it inevitable that he be placed in a position of defending his own work and to the extent that the Prosecution alleges that some of these constitutional amendments that he was involved in changing were made to reduce the rights of Kosovo Albanians, he would have an interest in saying no, there were legitimate legislative purposes for the work. Professor Markovic is therefore likely to be less objective than would a more disinterested outsider who did not have a personal stake in the materials at issue, and he has, because of his connection as I -- that I've outlined, a clear interest in the outcome of the case. He's not an independent expert. Additionally, in effect he was a de facto subordinate of Mr. Milutinovic. For example, one could see that during the negotiations in 1998 when Mr. Markovic was a member of the Serbian delegation, Mr. Milutinovic could announce publicly on the 14th of November that he would personally chair a meeting. Mr. Milutinovic could intervene and take over, and he did so. And I think the document is 1D88. And Mr. Milutinovic could do so because those persons, including Mr. Markovic -- sorry, Professor Markovic, were in fact his subordinates. And there's also the evidence from the Paris round of the negotiations in 1999 where Mr. Milutinovic took over the discussions from the other members of the Serbian delegation. In his report and in his testimony, Professor Markovic's approach offers an overly-hypothetical view of Mr. Milutinovic's authority. For example, he says that the law and the regulations in effect did not permit Mr. Milutinovic to represent Serbia in foreign affairs or to conduct any of its relations with foreign states or international organisations and persons. Well, perhaps the law said so, but the question is what was he doing at all these meetings? What was he doing at Rambouillet? What was he doing at Paris, where from all of the reports he took over the negotiations? So this is just an area that the Court should be alerted to, an overly technical and legalistic approach to the application of laws and there are many examples of that in this case. The Court, where necessary, should remove the shroud and to look at the reality of the situation. There -- there were other examples of Mr. Markovic's attempt to minimise Mr. Milutinovic's authority. In -- in regard to Article 87(3) [sic] of the constitution, if we could have that up, Mr. Markovic in his report, and even at the beginning of his evidence, was suggesting that this power, and I'm speaking about Article 83, subsection 7, power to adopt instruments at his own initiative or at the power of the government. Markovic suggested that this was belonging to the category of reserve powers and competencies and that the president could only exercise these powers if Serbia became an independent state. This was in his report 1D682, paragraph 226. When he was questioned about the reality of the situation in Serbia and including questions that emanated from the Bench, he was forced to admit that Markovic did and could exercise these powers and did so during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you mean Markovic or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that is a confusion. The accused Mr. Milutinovic. And I'm speaking about the testimony of Professor Markovic. Again, by an overstrict legalistic approach Professor Markovic seems to -- or attempts to minimise the reality of Mr. Milutinovic's authority, and it would be -- I would invite Your Honours, without going through all of that evidence, to review some of the evidence from Mr. Markovic, particularly at about transcript page 12900 and thereafter. Again Mr. -- Professor Markovic attempted to make a distinction, both in his report and in his testimony, between what the Supreme Defence Council could do. He said it could not decide upon anything. It could just state a position or adopt conclusions. And this -- in this area he is far, it is respectfully submitted, from being credible. His position is contrary to the natural meaning of the words in Article 135 of the FRY constitution in the Law on the VJ and the Law on the Defence and in the SDC's rules of procedure where it is stated that the SDC may make decisions and that the president of the FRY would manage or would command the army subject to the decisions of the SDC. And there are -- there's evidence before the Court where practically in reality, notwithstanding the legal niceties, where persons who were intimately associated with the SDC spoke of decisions or of its ability to make decisions. We had the evidence of General Dimitrijevic, whatever can be said about it, and much I'm sure will be said later on, that the SDC was the highest organ that was in control of the army and made the political decisions. We have the evidence of Momir Bulatovic who at one time was President of Montenegro, who testified that the SDC made the most important strategic decisions. And even within SDC meetings the record shows in P -- or 4D106 that there were occasions when even the Chief of the General Staff at the time, General Perisic, called on the SDC to make certain strategic decisions which he thought were important to enable the army to do what he thought they should do. So again this is an example of Markovic almost splitting hairs, as it were. Again, the objective being to minimise the authority of Mr. Milutinovic. The -- in respect to personnel matters, it is probably correct, as is stated in the Defence closing brief at paragraph 17, that technically the decision in respect to promotions of generals was within the legal ambit of the president of the FRY, President Milutinovic, President Milosevic.
