But even President Milosevic admitted during discussions that he had to bring it to the other members, and he would continue to bring it to the other members of the SDC for discussions even though technically and legally the power was vested in him. Mr. Milosevic could not have changed, chopped, and pruned the army as he liked, because he had to operate, had to operate, within the parameters, the strategic parameters, as set out and outlined for him by the Supreme Defence Council. Because of the nature of Mr. Milutinovic's power and authority, what is of fundamental importance is that, and this is insofar as the SDC is concerned, is that he had the material ability to convene meetings of SDC and to put on the agenda whatever he wanted to put. It is one thing for the Defence to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene. Could you augment by making a reference to any rule or law if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The rules of the SDC -- there were two rules of the SDC. It was amended on the 23rd of March. There you have it. The rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council of 1992 is P2622. This was a -- and Article 4 is the relevant article. This was amended immediately before the NATO intervention when a state of war was proclaimed on the 23rd of March. And the new rule which operated during that period is P1738, Article 4, which made certain changes, but one of -- one thing it did not change was the ability of an SDC member to request and insist upon a meeting being convened extraordinarily and to put an agenda item. So it's one thing for counsel on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic to say that yes, he was a member of the SDC but he did nothing, he did nothing in a positive way to further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think it would benefit if you read the rule straight away because then it will be registered well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have P1738 in e-court, Article 4. Okay, Article 5. Article 5 is the provision that enables him to put forward agenda proposals. "Members of the Supreme Defence Council or other participants may also put forward agenda proposals." Could we go to Article 3? I do apologise. When I first referred to the operative section I didn't have it before me. Now I could say that Article 3 empowers him to propose that a meeting convene, and Article 5 enables him to put whatever he might on the agenda. We also know from the evidence that as a matter of fact, although this was wartime, Mr. Milutinovic was meeting with Mr. Milosevic at least once a week. They said it was for a photo opportunity, to show that they -- the government -- there was a continuity in the government. So there were no logistical difficulties in saying to Mr. Milosevic as commander-in-chief of the VJ something like, "I went to Kosovo, and I was told by responsible people there that the allegations I am hearing in the international press that Albanians are being killed, murdered, and expelled whole-scale from Kosovo is correct. As a matter of fact, two senior leaders told me that. We need to convene a meeting of the SDC and to put the issue of the conduct of the VJ in this -- in the conduct of hostilities on the agenda." It was his duty and his right, and he was empowered to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But are you sure that he may not have done it at all, made no utterances or anything? Are you sure? Can you refer to something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Milutinovic -- and I will find the reference later on and I think this is conceded in the Defence trial brief that there were no meetings of the Supreme Defence Council during the period of hostilities, and indeed after May, June, July when the ICT indictment -- ICTY indictment became known to them. So that is not an issue in the case, and I will, with respect, Your Honour, find the precise reference in the Defence brief and bring it to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Another issue, and I can't go through them all, I will have to move rather quicker than I am now, another issue is Mr. Milutinovic's public pronouncement that he would act as guarantor of peace discussions or the political dialogue in 1998. I invite the Court to examine what he meant by this, examine what Markovic said it meant, and to apply it consistently, whatever being a guarantor means, to what was his duty in respect to the Kosovar Albanian population. According to the Milutinovic closing paragraph -- closing brief at paragraph 129, Mr. Milutinovic could act as a guarantor in his capacity as president to convene meetings and accompany state delegations to these meetings, to meet political leaders, diplomats, et cetera, and support the negotiation efforts. But Markovic -- Professor Markovic also explained what it meant, and the -- the extract is before the Court now. And I think in response to a question from the Court, if you could scroll down, an obvious question, if I may say so. The witness then tried to, again, when he saw the implications of what being a guarantor meant, he tried to restrict its meaning to -- to a moral position. So this is another example of Mr. -- of Professor Markovic telling you about his powers and immediately seeking to restrict it when he sees how it impacts on Mr. Milutinovic's position. And I will not read through this extract from the transcript. The duties implied by the oath of office of president are apparent and obvious despite the Milutinovic Defence argument that the oath was not a constitutional or legal norm and that non-compliance incurred no penalties. Markovic testified that it was mandatory that the president take the oath before becoming president. He could not choose his own words in assuming office, as was pointed out by one member of the Court. The mere fact that without the oath he cannot assume the office gives a legal shape to the requirement, and that is law. And this is at 12963 of the transcript. And even Markovic in his report, at paragraph 4 .5, summarised the effect, and the thing to focus on, that it was the guarantee -- it included a guarantee of compliance with the constitution and the law and the respect for human and civil rights. So not only did he have a role to guarantee and to protect state unity and integrity, but he had a role to protect his people, especially if they were endangered by organs of the state. His role as president was not that of an effete being. He was not merely decorative. We see, Your Honours, from the evidence that when he saw it fit to do so, he exercised himself in his role as guarantor by issuing public condemnations of the Kosovo Albanian leaders as irresponsible in their failure to attend a meeting that he attempted to convene, described them as amateur and transparent. And this is a public declaration that he made. And the relevant extract from 1D83 before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the issue of guaranteeing the outcome of the talks dealt with in your brief, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't think it is dealt with in any full way. Some of the documents are referred to, but not for this particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if we apply the reality of the principle of the president being a guarantor to the facts of this case, we ask ourselves what should he have done to comply or to guarantee compliance with the law and respect for human and civil rights when he was told by Merovci and Rugova about the oppression and violence committed against the Kosovo Albanian people. Could he not have publicly demanded that officials of the MUP report to him, or could he not have made that demand and if there was no satisfactory response make a similar public pronouncement? Had he not done -- had he done so, had he raised the alarm, could these crimes have been committed? Had he publicly and consistently pressured the perpetrators to desist and report, wouldn't during this relevant period wouldn't at least some of the perpetrators be arrested, be brought before the relevant court? The power he had as guarantor, the authority he had as guarantor, is even greater than his authority to guarantee a political dialogue, because he had to back it up. The constitutional power to demand from members of the government, including the MUP, a report. And we know that he knew that. And he did that on one occasion with respect to the Jashari incident. The Defence claims that he did not follow up on that because eventually he received a report that the killing of the Jashari family was committed in the course of legitimate police operations. However, I ask the Court to apply the principle consistently to a situation where there are these widespread crimes committed over a 78-day period. It is a submission that Mr. Markovic said, at 13 -- at transcript 13333 is not correct. He said that the president had no instruments at his disposal to make the government change its standpoint. All he can do is resign. Well, we know that Mr. Milutinovic did not. He remained there while these crimes were being committed. But there is clearly more that he could have done. The development of the joint criminal enterprise will be discussed, as I indicated, later on, and the Rambouillet negotiations are relevant there too, so I will come back to the Rambouillet discussions. There is one aspect I'd like to discuss because this particularly touches on the accused Mr. Milutinovic and not merely the overall joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Milutinovic is recorded in an Australian diplomatic correspondence to have said that bombing Serbia would lead to massacres. The evidence is before the Court of Ambassador Petritsch as to the circumstances in which this was made. Ambassador Petritsch testified about the care that was exercised in preparing these dispatches. The Defence suggests error. So I put before the Court the passage in which the report is made, and I submit to the Court that the possibility of error in this entire report about Mr. Milutinovic is minimal to the non-existent. The Defence suggested at 216 that one example of the error that might creep into these reports, because, of course, they were made at intense times, times of intense negotiations and difficult times, is -- and perhaps I should read it, but I will not. The only error that the Defence has found so far is a misspelling of a name. This is at page -- at paragraph 216 of their closing brief where the name Rossin, R-o-s-s-i-n, was misspelled as Rosen in the third paragraph of one of the dispatches, Exhibit P556. So the point I'm trying to make in maybe an overly convoluted way is that the Defence sought to suggest that because of the intensity of the situation when these reports, these diplomatic dispatches were being prepared, many of them were prepared early in the morning after intense talks, there was the possibility of error. I submit on the basis of the evidence of Ambassador Petritsch and Mr. Kickert as to how these dispatches are created, and if you look at the text of this dispatch, it does not admit in reality the possibility of error, and I further submit that the Defence example of an error which they posited at paragraph 256 of the closing brief is, yes, an error, but it is not an error of substance, the misspelling of a name in the third paragraph of the dispatch which is the subject of P556. The Defence further claims that Mr. Petritsch's record of Mr. Milutinovic's comment in the dispatch is not reliable because he failed to mention it when he was interviewed by the OTP in May. Your Honour, I think experience including in this case will tell us that the absence of a particular reference in a statement does not foreclose the issue as to whether or not something happened. We have seen on many occasions, both with Defence witnesses and with Prosecution witnesses, important matters coming out in what has been become known in this case as supplementary information sheets. The interview in May was also conducted in intense circumstances, and it is the submission of the Prosecution that a contemporaneous record, a record made hours after the event in question, in the circumstances described by Mr. Petritsch is likely to be accurate and have a regard to other evidence in this case. It is accurate. The point made at paragraph 218 that Mr. Kickert did not say anything during his interview or when he was present at Mr. Petritsch's interview in May about this comment by Milutinovic is not consequential because Kickert said that he was not present at the meeting when Mr. Milutinovic made the statement. Also at paragraph 221, the Defence seems to be saying that Petritsch never spoke to Milutinovic. I don't think this was put to Mr. Petritsch when he testified, and the Defence had the opportunity to point this out -- point it out on the record if it was in fact so put. The other point the Defence makes in respect to this statement at paragraph 20 -- or 220 of their closing is that Mr. Petritsch transposed Stambuk's statement to Mr. Milutinovic. If Your Honours will recall Milutinovic had sent in a statement that Stambuk said so and he said that in the course of the Milosevic trial as well. When he came here for this trial, his memory was refreshed by his contemporaneous record in the dispatch that was made hours after which he had not seen at any of those occasions because they were only recently made available. And he did forthrightly concede that he did not remember Mr. Milutinovic saying it, but having regard to their standards in preparing these dispatches, the possibility that that could be incorrect was negligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me, Mr. Stamp. Did Mr. Petritsch say that he actually heard the statement being made --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- by Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. He said -- he said that the record that he sees here causes him to accept that he heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought he said had no personal recollection of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He had no recollection of hearing it, but the record -- he's prepared to accept the record that he made that he heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So he's relying entirely on the record. It is mere speculation to suggest that Mr. Petritsch was transposing what Stambuk said to Mr. Milutinovic, and this is merely making out Mr. Petritsch to be confused in his record-keeping. Your Honours, there is no lack of knowledge or mystery in the fact that two persons, two leading members of a Serbian state may make substantially a statement of that nature. The evidence before the Court is that Seselj made a similar statement. This is discussed at the Prosecution pre-trial brief at page 406. Rugova in his testimony in Milosevic said Milutinovic substantially said the same thing to him. The reason for the problem that -- with Albania is because of the NATO bombing. So that type of comment had become a slogan, a sort of mantra for many of the people who were in the leadership of the FRY, and I think indeed Mr. Rugova testified to that in the -- in the Milosevic case. That this was not something that was not -- that was -- he was hearing for the first time. There are some other aspects of the Milutinovic matter which I may return to with leave of the Court if time permits. I'd like to invite the Court to review the evidence as discussed in the Prosecution closing brief, and I submit that the evidence there is comprehensive and is conclusive and is evidence that the Court is entitled to act on. If I may move on to -- to make some submissions in respect to the accused Mr. Sainovic. There is a significant amount of evidence in respect to the conduct of Mr. Sainovic and his participation in the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise. The Defence thesis boils down to this: Firstly, his role in Kosovo in 1998 and up to the NATO intervention arose entirely from his position of being a federal deputy prime minister with responsibility for foreign affairs. As a matter of fact, I think the Defence went on to suggest that it was because of this role that he was there in the first place. They say that he was involved in and sent out to Kosovo to work in the field of foreign affairs due to the rising number of foreign diplomats in Kosovo after the 16th of June, 1998. The second part of the Defence thesis in respect of Mr. Sainovic is that as far as 1999 is concerned, as far as the indictment period is concerned, apart from four events and his connection with respect to activities with Mr. Rugova, there's nothing to link him to Kosovo. And the Defence tries to make an entirely artificial separation between the different periods, as if the conduct and circumstances that prevailed in one period, in a preceding period, did not have an impact on the succeeding period, but I will come to that later on. The first contention that he went to Kosovo and was involved in Kosovo in 1998, up to the NATO intervention because of the foreign presence there, because the presence of foreign diplomats, rings hollow when one considers other evidence that the Defence fails to address. Sainovic at an earlier state, before the foreign diplomats arrived for their work in KDOM and the KVM mission had been sent down to Kosovo and was involved in matters concerning Kosovo, and these were not dealings with foreign affairs or foreign diplomats. For instance, in his interview with the OTP, that is P605, he states that shortly after the Jashari incident in early 1998, he participated in a meeting with five or six Albanian representatives held in the premises of the Democratic Alliance of Kosovo in Pristina. That is Rugova's headquarters. This is sometime before what the Defence is saying that caused him to go down there, the KDOM mission in June. The Albanian delegation at that time was headed by Fehmi Agani and the Serb delegation was led, ostensibly at least, by Ratko Markovic. This is at page 26 of his interview, P605. At page 28 he confirms that there was no international presence at the meeting, although he said that there were -- there was international attention regarding Kosovo, and there was some foreign role in the preparation of the meeting. So the Defence -- and it is not a matter of principle or a submission or an argument. The Defence is factually incorrect, it is submitted. Further on at page 29 of his interview, Sainovic states that he and past president or former president Lilic were charged with going to Kosovo, and I quote: "Were charged with going to Kosovo to get our own, to monitor, to observe the situation there and to gain an insight into the situation." According to Mr. Sainovic, they went on two two-day visits -- or, actually, on two one-day visits to the most critical areas in Kosovo, Pec, Djakovica at the time, and border military posts. In Pec, they met various representatives of various departments from Klina and Istok. This -- or these outings with Mr. Lilic took place shortly after the meetings in Pristina in April 1998, and they are discussed -- or he describes these meetings at pages 29 to 33 of his -- of his statement. So Sainovic's role in Kosovo in 1998 is a little bit more than what is suggested by the Defence. Next the Defence suggests that it was entirely an independent decision on the part of federal Prime Minister at the time Bulatovic to dispatch him to Kosovo because of the foreign presence there. Your Honours are aware that it is the Prosecution's case, as Mr. Hannis outlined earlier this morning, that the mastermind of the joint criminal enterprise was Mr. Milosevic, who controlled the strings, who employed and dismissed, who appointed, who placed the individuals where he wanted them placed. Mr. Sainovic, in his submission at paragraph 44 and thereafter, quite a few paragraphs, says that the sending of Sainovic to Kosovo and Metohija was the independent decision of Mr. Bulatovic. Bulatovic wrote this about sending Sainovic to Kosovo and Metohija in his book, he said: "Slobodan Milosevic had two specific demands on me concerning personnel. "Milosevic's second request was to charge Sainovic ... with running political activities relating to ... Kosovo ..." Demands, that is what he wrote, demands that Mr. Milosevic had. Now, when Mr. Bulatovic first came to testify or came here to testify, he claimed that the decision to send Mr. Sainovic to Kosovo was entirely his. Later on, he said in the context of the politics at the time it was his decision and Mr. Milosevic agreed after he made the decision. Mr. Hannis in cross-examination showed him this passage from the book. He -- I don't know how to describe it. I can only ask Your Honours to re-read his answers at 3896 to 8. He said that what he said in the book was true. Milosevic did make the demand but it was really his decision. I think he goes on to explain that only he had the legal and formal power to make the decision to appoint him. Well, yes, we know that, but it comes back to what I implore the Court to always keep in mind, that it is the reality of the configuration and deployment of power and its exercise that matters and not in all cases legal niceties. I recall the situation arose in court where the question came up how was it that Mr. Milosevic, when he was President of Serbia with the same constitutional trappings, was so powerful, could do so much? He could because of various realities. Similarly, I ask the Court to look to the reality. The Milosevic effect and domination of these appointments in Kosovo is further confirmed by the evidence in respect to Mr. Loncar's appointment. If we look at paragraph 15 of his statement, page 25 -- sorry, P2521, he discusses how -- sorry, this is paragraph 14. In that paragraph he discusses how he came to be appointed. The last sentence is the important one. He said that: "Since Milosevic wanted me on this council, he said that he would instruct Bulatovic to include me." Well, of course, Mr. -- or General Loncar was duly appointed. The Prosecution accepts that when Mr. Bulatovic appointed General Loncar he had the relevant constitutional power to do so, but this was Mr. Milosevic's appointment in reality. Interestingly, I should point out to the Court that somewhat similar to Mr. Bulatovic, when Mr. Loncar came to testify here, he -- he sought to -- to dilute the plain meaning of what he had said in a statement. If one looks at the evidence that was read over to him and that he confirmed, he seeks to express uncertainty about Milosevic using the word "instruct," and it is somehow diluted. But I think that the evidence shows that at least that it was at Mr. Milosevic's instigation that all of these persons were appointed to the various positions they held in Kosovo. He did, in effect, an agree to the proposition that it was Mr. Milosevic who initiated it. This raises another issue that I'll return to later, but I could highlight now because of these two examples. It has not been entirely uncommon in this case that some witnesses who have come to testify to the Court have sought to dilute or negate statements that they made earlier or official records that they made or the records of statements that they made in formal and official circumstances. We recently heard General Dimitrijevic deny that he told Mr. Crosland that he did not agree with actions taken by the security forces in Kosovo since Sainovic had taken over and that Mr. Sainovic was overriding the wishes of the General Staff. We saw before this Court official records of the collegium meetings of the VJ in which General Dimitrijevic, in a role and in a context where he was -- had a responsibility to make accurate reports and accurate statements because it involved the lives of his troops, the record has him saying not even Sainovic or any other Sainovic can solve the problems by lightly deciding to use his units. This is another example of later on when he comes to court he says, no, the record is incorrect. Similarly, Djakovic sought to minimise or qualify the natural meanings, the meaning of the words that he used when he made a record of the -- of the Joint Command meetings. This is an important exhibit, an important document, a record made a senior officer at the command of the corps commander that he maintain a record, and he says he was trying to convert words spoken by laymen to military-speak. The Prosecution submits that the -- these official records, in the circumstance of this case, may be relied upon by the Trial Chamber and not discarded as a -- as counsel for Mr. Sainovic submits. And they may be relied upon notwithstanding the later evidence of these many witnesses. These are contemporaneous records made officially sometimes in the course of a duty to -- to advise carefully and accurately. There is nothing to indicate that they were self-serving or that there were reasons for the makers to misrepresent the truth when they were making these records. Having said that, I wish to turn to P1468, a document which will be discussed more fully by Mr. Hannis when he comes to speak about the Joint Command. This is a record of the Joint Command meetings by Mr. Djakovic. The Defence claims that the purpose of these meetings was an exchange of information, and that's in paragraph 74, and that Mr. Sainovic only spoke about matters involving foreign affairs or political matters. I invite the Court to consider P1468 notwithstanding Djakovic's evidence that he was translating what laymen were saying into military-speak. And it is the submission of the Prosecution that this record speaks for itself. These examples prove unambiguously that Mr. Sainovic was not speaking merely about politics and foreign affairs, and they could not constitute an erroneous or mistaken record. Djakovic could not have made this type of mistake when he wrote down what Mr. Sainovic was saying. And these are orders or approval given to military exercises, and this confirms the Prosecution's case that Sainovic's role in Kosovo was to exercise political oversight over the forces of the FRY. Now, if we look at all of them, you know, the words of some politicians might be shrouded in mystery, full of conundrums, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, by political oversight, what do you mean? Under his auspices or what do you mean by oversight?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: His role was a role that was charted by Mr. Milosevic to control and approve what was done by the force of the FRY in Kosovo. The Prosecution's case is that he was not a foot soldier. He was not involved directly in the chains of command of the police or the army in a direct way, and that is why I use the term "political oversight." He had the power, though, to approve their operations or to insist that some operations be undertaken, although he was not involved necessarily or there was no need for him to be involved in how these operations took place and the mechanics of these operations. And it is submitted that if that is borne in mind, then some of the rhetorical questions that are -- that one finds in the Sainovic closing brief as to why if Sainovic was in command he did not attend these military meetings and why if he was in command he did not attend these police meetings, in his answer he's not a soldier and he's not a policeman. He's not out in the field conducting operations. That is somebody else's department. Different elements are responsible for their own -- for implementation of their own part or parts of the JCE, but he has overall control because he is the confidant, the political confidant of Mr. Milosevic in Kosovo and that was well known. That, Your Honour, is discussed, the fact that it was well known by a variety of people in Kosovo at the time is discussed in the Prosecution's closing brief. I don't have the precise citation of the paragraph in the crossing brief, but that was the understanding of many people who had to work in Kosovo at the time. One must recall when -- when assessing Djakovic's evidence that perhaps there might be errors in the records that he made and in considering Defence's submission that the records should be discarded, that Djakovic was also a member of the Joint Command, and he also does have an interest to minimise the role of the Joint Command in the -- in some of the operations. The Joint Command at that time was not a body that was set up under any legal or constitutional authority. I invite the Court, without going through the details, to review Loncar's evidence in respect to Sainovic. He -- perhaps I could ask the Court to have a brief look at this. Loncar, in his statement P2521, paragraph 28, you look at the first paragraph -- that's paragraph 38 before the Court, it's a general, former general in the VJ posted in Kosovo. He says: "I do not know about the nature of Sainovic's contacts with these people, but I assume it had something to do with the fact that Sainovic was responsible for Kosovo. I presume it was Milosevic that was giving him the authority." When he came here to testify, asked that the expression "de facto" be inserted to qualify what he was saying about Mr. Sainovic's authority, the fact that Mr. Sainovic was responsible for Kosovo, and in his testimony at 7603 to 4, he effectively confirmed that the de facto situation was that Sainovic had authority from Milosevic in Kosovo. So Loncar at least gives credible evidence about Sainovic's power and his work in Kosovo, and that evidence contradicts the Defence claim at paragraph 64 of its final trial brief that Sainovic -- Sainovic's power and role are roles from his office of deputy prime minister with responsible -- responsibility for foreign affairs. It was Loncar's evidence, again this is discussed in the Prosecution's brief, that Sainovic tried to do much, much more than his various legal functions strictly compelled him to do. There were attacks on -- on Mr. Ciaglinski in respect to his statements. This is -- much of this has been set out in the Prosecution's closing brief. The evidence of Mr. Ciaglinski and his ability to make a judgement as to Sainovic's position, it is submitted, is clearly set out in the brief. There's also an attack on the General -- we'll describe as General DZ who expressed the opinion that Sainovic was in charge of Kosovo. Your Honours, to save time I will not go through, as I didn't plan to. That attack -- much of that again is discussed in the closing brief. I just would like to remind the Court that General DZ could and did give specific incidences where -- which demonstrated to him that Sainovic was exercising effective power and control in -- in Kosovo. So, I think a careful analysis of the evidence explodes the Defence thesis that Sainovic went down there at the behest of the federal Prime Minister Bulatovic to be engaged in diplomatic affairs. And then we come to the NATO bombing. As I indicated, it's an entirely artificial separation to say that we should chunk these time frames into different periods and -- and not consider how one impacts on another. One of the fundamental, and this is by way of example, one of the fundamental aspects of the Prosecution's case is that the knowledge by the participants of the excessive force employed by the force of the FRY in 1998 impacted on their state of mind and is evidence of their intention in 1999, because they would have known if they unleashed those same forces in similar circumstances with even less control, then similar and worse than occurred in 1998 would have occurred in 1999. So there cannot be a too strict separation of these periods, the events involved to some degree. I'd like to put before the Court something that one might call Sainovic's time line in 1999. I'll do it, perhaps it's unnecessary. I do it because in opening the Defence case, Mr. Fila, on behalf of Mr. Sainovic, suggested at transcript 13791 that during that period Mr. Sainovic spent so much time outside of Kosovo that it would be absurd to suggest that he had any influence or control of the events in Kosovo. I remind the Court of evidence set out in the pre-trial brief that Sainovic was not engaged in the day-to-day and direct operation of the forces in the field, and I ask you -- or I submit to you that if you look at his appearances in Kosovo, one will see that for his role, his political role, he was there on sufficient occasions to exercise that, and that the Defence evidence, which I'm sure you'll be directed to, that he was primarily or almost entirely engaged in Bor, in his home municipality of Bor during that period is not to be accepted, or at least he did find enough time to travel and to remain in Kosovo at critical points during a war. There are, Your Honours, other meetings I have noted here but did not put it here. We have before the Court -- or evidence of Obrad Stevanovic's work notebook, P1898, where he spoke of another meeting in Milosevic's office that was attended by Stevanovic and Sainovic in May 1999 where the task of mopping up the terrain was discussed. I should point out in this time line those and the meetings of the 4th of May and the 17th of May, were meetings in Belgrade. I will check to correct myself. I think the meeting on the 4th of May was a meeting in Kosovo where Mr. Sainovic escorted Mr. Rugova to Belgrade and the meeting on the 17th of May was entirely Belgrade. Mr. Sainovic did have time and opportunity, contrary to what the Defence was submitting. The -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder -- I wonder, Mr. Stamp, if we can deal with that after lunchtime. Would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we will adjourn now for an hour, and we will resume at a quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May it please you. The question arises in respect to the period of the NATO intervention is what was Sainovic -- Mr. Sainovic doing at these meetings that he attended. According to the reports of the meetings we have, Sainovic's role was the role of someone who was attuned with the operations of the security forces in Kosovo and was exercising civilian control over them. If we look at the meeting of the 4th of April, 1999, of the MUP staff, notwithstanding the Defence claim in its closing brief that Sainovic's visit did not have any implication on the work of the MUP, the Court, it is respectfully submitted, can review what he said at this meeting. This is the meeting of the 4th of April, 1999, and the minutes are in P1989. And among the things that Sainovic said, if I may quote: "It is necessary for the first stage of the anti-terrorist operations to be completed today for the purpose of active defence and for the protection of the territory and the border in case of a breakthrough by the aggressor deep into the territory of the FRY." Cvetic, the witness Cvetic was present at the meeting and testified at transcript 8081 in a manner which was consistent with the -- with the minutes that I just mentioned, but that he was even stronger. He said that Sainovic pointed out that all planned operations had to be concluded by that day and that the MUP would thereafter move on to other tasks. So Sainovic was giving directives at these meetings. If we look at the meeting of the 7th of May, the MUP meeting, and the record of that meeting which is P1996, we see that Minister Sainovic gave a very long speech. The speech did cover political matters. It did cover matters involving other areas outside of security, but it also had statements in it that only someone who was intimately involved with the operation of the security forces and had a capacity or responsibility to direct their work would say. At page 2 of P1996, which is the minutes for the 7th of May, 1999, MUP staff meeting, he stated that the KLA had been destroyed in anti-terrorist combat and operations conducted by the police force, and then: "After Operation Jezerce there will no longer be a large terrorist stronghold except for 30 to 40 smaller-scale strongholds numbering 500 to 700 terrorists in areas in which the secretariats themselves will destroy and completely neutralise them." Later on he said, and this is in the nature of a directive, after, that is: "After Operation Jezerce, all detachments of PJP units will return to their secretariats and in cooperation with the VJ work on destroying the remaining terrorist groups. In addition to destroying the so-called KLA and terrorists, the main objective of anti-terrorist operations would be to ensure peace in Kosovo and Metohija." Again at page 3 he told them that: "The relationship of the VJ and the police had been defined and settled and this is functioning well and detachments are returning to places where they are stationed on the territory of the secretariats of the interior in the entire region of Kosovo and Metohija in order to maintain law and order." Page 4, he speaks about the Yugoslav army and he says: "The Yugoslav army has been ordered that all units be subordinated -- all VTO units be subordinated to VJ brigades with the tasks of working to protect the features, roads, et cetera, outside towns." So this is -- this is a record of a participation in meeting which goes well beyond that of a foreign affairs plenipotentiary. He is intimately aware of what is going on and he is giving directions or at least approval of plans, at least approval of plans for future action. This is within his role as a political director, political operative. The -- there was a lot of testimony about his presence and participation at the meeting on the 17th of May, too much to review here, but of course -- but at least I ask the Court to consider the question of what was he doing in a meeting of this nature on the 17th of May? What would his role be? It was held at the command post of the Supreme Command in Belgrade. The other participants were President Milosevic, General Ojdanic, Rade Markovic the head of the DB -- RDB, General Pavkovic, General Farkas, Colonel Gajic, General Vasiljevic. These are the prominent -- or some of the prominent members, most prominent members in the security forces and President Milosevic. So Sainovic was the only politician there with Milosevic, and it is respectfully submitted that it is inconceivable that one could submit that his presence there is for any role involving foreign affairs. Indeed, Your Honours, it is apparent that his role there must have been as a result of his responsibility for the operations of the security forces. And the comments that he is reported to have made at this meeting demonstrate that he's well informed and that he exercised authority and influence. Your Honours are quite entitled to draw appropriate inferences from the evidence as to what his authority was. According to Vasiljevic and the notes he took, Sainovic made statements including, "We have ordered that reports be submitted in all sectors about what's happening and what needs to be investigated." And he spoke of the task of working on cleaning up the terrain. He said that it would be good if someone else got engaged down there like some kind of a supervisor. He spoke further, according to Vasiljevic, of problems they were having down there with the uniforms of some groups and the difficulties in controlling persons wearing certain uniforms. This is in P2592. He -- in regard to reports that Arkan's men were being sent to Kosovo Polje, Mr. Sainovic said he would check out the veracity of the report. Pavkovic suggested forming a body to investigate the allegations made against the MUP and the VJ, and Sainovic agreed, according to Vasiljevic. When Vasiljevic reported that the SAJ was integrating into their force groups such as the Skorpions which had not previously fulfilled requirements for serving in the MUP and that they had been brought to Serbia -- or brought to Kosovo, Sainovic commented that it was obvious that the SAJ had its own habits when it came to forming the reserves. Lastly, last example, according to Vasiljevic there was a preliminary meeting on the 16th of May, 1999, and at that meeting Pavkovic said that he had informed Sainovic that a group of Skorpions and Boca in Prolom Banja wearing NATO-type uniforms and the insignia of SAJ were active. Pavkovic had also said that he had had ordered the military organs to establish responsibility in respect to these bodies and that he had informed Mr. Sainovic about everything that he had done. Why, the question arises, would it be the responsibility -- would Pavkovic have that responsibility to inform -- of informing Sainovic of these types of operations? You have heard a lot of evidence on the meeting of the 1st of June, 1999. The meeting was discussed by General Vasiljevic. It is set out in his evidence in P2600. And before this screen is 2D387 which I will get to, but P2600 I also comment for Your Honours' consideration. This is Mr. Vasiljevic's original statement about that meeting which he accepted when he came to testify first and basically said that this was a meeting where Generals Lazarevic and Lukic gave reports. The meeting was presided over by Pavkovic. And having heard the report and heard the plans, Pavkovic -- sorry. May I repeat the proposal -- the submission I was making. This was a meeting where, among others, General Lazarevic and General Lukic submitted reports with plans and proposals. Mr. Sainovic was present, presided over the meeting, and Mr. Sainovic expressed approval of the plans. And the evidence in P2600 on that meeting is quite clear. It is true that later on an attempt was -- well, that later on the Defence submitted another statement from General Vasiljevic in respect of that meeting in which some of the points in respect to Sainovic's role are not made as strongly and that statement, almost the entirety of it, is before the Court now. Nonetheless, in this last statement General Vasiljevic did agree that Sainovic accepted and agreed that everything that he had heard should be proceeded with as planned. So again, as is not uncommon, we'll see there was some dilution of the evidence, but nonetheless, nonetheless, the essential elements still exist in regard to this part or this aspect of the evidence. The pre-trial brief discusses clear the meeting with Rugova. Maybe one comment I could make in respect of that meeting is Merovci testified that during all of these meetings, and there were several, it was clear that Mr. Sainovic was receiving instructions and applying instructions from Mr. Milutinovic. There are some quick matters in respect of Mr. Sainovic which I will move through. The Defence in submitting that Mr. Sainovic was helpful and presented a helpful face in the negotiating party for the group from Serbia and the FRY at Rambouillet and other discussions referred to the evidence of Mr. Byrnes. The point the Defence is trying to make is that Mr. Byrnes is saying that Mr. Sainovic is sincere. The other point that the Defence is trying to make is Mr. Sainovic is not in control. If one looks at the evidence of Mr. Byrnes and this is quoted quite fully in paragraphs 550 to 551 of the Sainovic closing brief, Mr. Byrnes is saying that he remembered distinctly pushing Mr. Sainovic to try to get the Serbian delegation to be more flexible as it was his view that the NATO threat of bombing Serbia was not a bluff and Serbia was unlikely to get a better deal than what they were being offered at Rambouillet. And he distinctly remembered Mr. Sainovic sitting there thoughtfully and finally responding to my question with words something to the effect that he did not have the authority to be that flexible, that there were too many constraints imposed on him by Belgrade, and at the end of the day, there was nothing he could do in that direction. This shows as the Prosecution submitted in the indictment and pre-trial brief that he was political head. He's speaking about what he can do and what he can't do, and he speaks of the directions he gets from Belgrade. Indeed the evidence is that in the course of the Rambouillet discussions he was the one who was permitted to leave, to return to Belgrade to consult with Mr. Milosevic. Further evidence from Mr. Petritsch which is accepted by the Defence in their pre-trial brief from paragraphs 535 and thereafter is that Mr. Sainovic was the one they could go to to salvage the negotiations where there appeared to be insurmountable difficulties, two times in particular, one at the beginning of the talks, one at the end when they needed to get the -- the Serbian group to budge. It was Mr. Sainovic they went to and Mr. Sainovic who did his magic, so to speak. The Defence raises these points, I think, to suggest that he was malleable, but they also show the core submission of the Prosecution, that it was he who was politically in charge and that he could get things or get changes made. A huge broadside was made against the character of the witness Cvetic. He was the only SUP witness who testified -- or SUP chief who testified on behalf of the Prosecution and he took -- he gave evidence about the Joint Command, about Mr. Sainovic and his role and about the role of Mr. Lukic. And his evidence, it is submitted, is important evidence. The attack on his credibility is made primarily in respect to his evidence that at a meeting of July -- of June or July 1998 either Mr. Djordjevic or Mr. Obrad Stevanovic announced that a Joint Command had been set up and that the members of the Joint Command included Mr. Sainovic. I see it was the testimony of Cvetic was at a MUP meeting of the 22nd of July, 1998, Djordjevic announced the formation of the Joint Command and that Sainovic, Minic, Lukic, and Pavkovic composed the command. His credibility is attacked. It is said that this is not mentioned in the minutes of that meeting. Your Honours, I invite the Court to have a look at the minutes of that meeting. It is 6D798. These so-called minutes comprise a page and a half of notes. We have seen minutes of MUP meetings, and it is obvious that this is incomplete. Indeed when it was shown to the witness Mijatovic, Mijatovic in spite of his -- his own credibility issues indeed was the one who used the word "obvious," "obviously incomplete," he said in answer to questions about those minutes at 22315 to 6 of the transcript. Cvetic was also attacked because Mr. Mijatovic who was at that meeting said, well, he did not hear any such thing. A slew -- many witnesses were called by the Defence, former members of the police in Kosovo to testify, and many of them forgot about the Joint Command. Some didn't know it. Many of them gave highly questionable evidence about what the Joint Command was. Mr. Hannis will more fully address that. However, I point out that Mr. Mijatovic is not the type of witness that one should use to attack the credibility of one such as Cvetic. He was the witness it should be recalled who in the course of his testimony had to be reminded by the Trial Chamber about his solemn undertaking to speak the truth and warned of consequences, and this was in respect to his testimony about the minutes of that meeting. Again Vucurevic and Adamovic were witnesses who testified at that meeting, that is Dusko Adamovic -- sorry. They were persons who testified here about that meeting, and they claim that they heard no such thing. Again, these are not credible witnesses. I would invite the Court to review the excellent cross-examination of Mr. Adamovic by counsel for Pavkovic. Mr. Pavkovic -- Mr. Adamovic started out by saying that he knew very little about the liaison between the MUP and the VJ, and it took the able efforts of counsel to eventually get him to agree that not only did he know about it but he was the main liaison who was passing over the maps. Not, it is respectfully submitted, a credible witness. So these are the -- Bogunovic is another person who was not present at that meeting but who came and in response to very leading questions by counsel accepted that Cvetic was a bad man, a bad superior, a man who was locked up in his office. Bogunovic, be it recalled, was the witness who failed to remember that he attended a meeting of the MUP described in P1996, where he even delivered a report which is recorded. He denied giving that report although the minutes have been clearly -- have him down clearly as a participant. Many of these witnesses, Your Honours, many of the testimonies given by the Defence witnesses who were subordinates of Mr. Lukic or Mr. Lazarevic or General Pavkovic is not -- is the evidence of persons who are not credible. Your Honour, there were -- or is there a series of rhetorical questions at paragraph 617 of the Sainovic closing brief I had intended to address but I think, Your Honour, and I would submit that if one starts from the position that Mr. Sainovic was not a soldier, he was not a policeman, he was not there in the day-to-day operations on the ground, then these questions become redundant, and the other questions about why, if he was there in a political role to coordinate why there were problems in resubordination of the MUP, problems with the coordination itself as is indicated by the case of the evidence, are questions which -- which are not -- well, which the answer is -- I'll answer the question. Milutinovic -- not Milutinovic, Mr. Milosevic, who is accepted by all here to be the person who had dominant power, he, too, had problems with the subordination. He, too, had to issue an order in respect to the subordination. This order was not specifically complied with for a long period of time. So the fact that there were problems with resubordination does not mean that Sainovic did not have a role and did not have authority, because even Milosevic had problems with that when the real circumstances of war confronted him. So those questions, I think, are not questions that present any real difficulty. The evidence in respect to Mr. Sainovic is clear that he exercised real authority, and again as the situation applies to Mr. Milutinovic, I respectfully submit and ask the Court to look to the reality, the reality as described by the witnesses and not to the facade of the technical niceties which the Defence would present. I -- we had indicated that we would move immediately to Mr. Lukic, but I think we have decided to stick by the order and to deal with the military witnesses and then get back to Mr. Lukic and also the general comments about the evidence. Thank you very much, Your Honours, may it please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just to clarify something for my understanding. Now, you said that he had the powers not only what you called them as a political -- for political overseeing, but also for bringing about changes. Could you help me understand this a little more by -- if you kindly could refer to something to help me in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When I spoke about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The changes you said. He could bring changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When I spoke about the changes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, because you say -- I'm sorry, I'm interrupting. When we heard, when we saw one of the excerpts from a statement with respect to him being told by the VJ and MUP about things and, yes, he agreed that's what is said, but then later commenting you said he could even bring about changes. Now, that I don't know. I'm a little confused about it. Can you clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: With reference to something tangible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When I spoke about him effecting changes, I was speaking about his role at the negotiations at Rambouillet. The Defence in their closing brief sought to suggest that Mr. Sainovic was in fact a helpful partner in the negotiation process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, but that you thought was his role as having the foreign affairs with him. But when you talked of changes, you didn't mean changes which were in certain planning or in something which was organised by VJ or by MUP? You didn't mean that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. I was referring to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. No, it's clear. If you're only referring to that, but not to other changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But then you see the point is that he was agreeing to certain plans which were put up before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So would you like to say anything about any other overt act in this respect coming from his side?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see -- we see primarily in his role in 1998 which continued, it is submitted, and I had put before the Court many examples of the -- of what he's recorded as having said at these Joint Command meetings. Many of them, it is the Prosecution's submission, are unequivocally instructions, instructions as to what the security forces need to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: When he said conclude it in such-and-such time or do it in certain time, that's what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will now turn to General Ojdanic. General Ojdanic was the top soldier, the highest ranking uniformed member of the VJ from his appointment as chief of the VJ General Staff on 24 November 1998. He was also chief of the Supreme Command Staff during the war from 24 March 1999. In that position he was the VJ's representative at the Supreme Defence Council meetings. He had de jure and de facto command over the VJ subordinated units. And we say he contributed to the joint criminal enterprise in various ways. He directed VJ combat operations. He was involved in the arming of non-Siptars. He played a role in the Supreme Defence Council and Supreme Command. He participated in violation of the October agreements, and he also contributed to the JCE by failing to take certain actions regarding General Pavkovic. Now, first I want to talk about some of the directives that were issued by General Ojdanic and the Supreme -- well, the General Staff and the Supreme Command Staff both before and during the war. The first one I would like you to look at or refer to is Grom 3 directive on the 16th of January, 1999. This is Exhibit 3D690. I'm also going to look after that at the 9 April 1999 directive which is P1481, and the 29 May directive P1465. But let's start with Grom 3, 3D690. This was General Ojdanic's directive dated the 16th of January, 1999, and it's described as being "to prevent introduction by force of a multinational NATO brigade." In that document we saw that the task for the 3rd Army, at least in stage two of the directive, was to "destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Kosovo and Metohija." And subsequent to this directive issued by General Ojdanic, it's followed up by General Pavkovic as command of the 3rd Army and when he issued his own Grom 3 order on the 27th of January, 1999, which was not only to prevent the NATO brigade being introduced but also for "destruction of Siptar terrorist forces in Kosovo." Now, the Grom 3 from General Pavkovic is Exhibit 5D245. As I said, dated the 27th of January. The phase 2 task assigned to the Pristina Corps by General Pavkovic was "to destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in Kosovo." And in item 5.1 of that order we saw that the Pristina Corps was to "engage the armed non-Siptar population, to secure military features and communication routes, and for the defence of populated areas with non-Siptar population." Subsequent to the issues of that Grom 3 order, about four days later General Pavkovic issued an order to the Pristina Corps and General Lazarevic to carry out various tasks. One of those is found at item 5 in that exhibit, 5D49, and the Pristina Corps ordered to draft a plan for "destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the Drenica, Lab and Malisevo sectors." This plan was also to ensure complete coordination with MUP units and was ordered to be done by 15 February 1999. And in evidence we have Exhibit P2808. We say, Your Honours, this is Lazarevic's version of Grom 3 pursuant to the order by General Pavkovic. You may recall that Exhibit P2808 is a rather lengthy order by General Lazarevic to break up and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the sector of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo, and it's -- it carries the strictly confidential number 455-1. You will recall we had a lot of discussion and a lot of evidence about the numbering of these Pristina Corps documents, and the Joint Command orders that we see from the 22nd of March and thereafter all bore that number 455. So this is the first in that series related to the Joint Command orders which we say led to the crimes charged in the indictment. This order also indicated that the subordinates receiving the order were to engage armed non-Siptars to secure military facilities and communications and defend places with non-Siptar populations. Just as an example of how this order was carried out further down the line, in item 5.5 there is a task for the 549th Motorised Brigade under Colonel Delic to carry out a blockade along with parts of Battle Group 21, and if you'll make a note, Your Honours, if you care to see how that is followed through later on, Exhibits P2015, 1981 and 1995 will allow you to track how the order gets from the very top down to the ground level. Now, related to this we see something that appears to be on the MUP side, and that is a document dated the 19th of February, three days later. This is Exhibit number 6D716. It's titled "MUP staff," and it is an order "to break up and destroy forces of Albanian terrorists in the sector of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo." And if you look at it side by side with General Lazarevic's P2808, you will see it echos the task called for there. This was a bit of a mystery for all of us I think until Colonel Djakovic came and testified, I guess General Djakovic now, and told us that this was a document that was drafted by him. You'll find that in transcript at page 26930. He told us it was drafted by him and given by him to Dusko Adamovic from the MUP. And he told us in answering a question asked by you, Mr. President, that this is a form -- a form of order, because, after all, we have to admit that the army was more trained from that point of view in terms of writing such documents so we simply wanted to help, to help the members of the MUP so that they could formulate these documents as they should be formulated in tentative terms. And if you look at the particular task contained within that document, for example, in item 1 you'll see a task for the 22nd Detachment of the PJP where they were going to be supported by Battle Group 211, Colonel Gergar. And you will see in items 5.13 and 5.14 task in the area of Bela Crkva by the 549th and the 549th Brigade, the 243rd, and the 37th PJP Detachment, which line up later with the crimes that occurred at the beginning of the NATO campaign. Now, further support of that was from the testimony of Colonel Zivaljevic from the PJP who talked about having seen the content of this order in his meeting with Colonel Gergar and having received a map extract, and he told us that he recognised all the details in that exhibit as being what he was given to carry out later on when he actually engaged in operations in Kosovo. P1966 is one of our first Joint Command orders at the -- right at the beginning of the conflict which called for routing and destroying the Siptar terrorists in the Malo Kosovo area pursuant to that original Grom 3 order. That's strictly confidential number 455-56. And you'll recall that that was the one to which General Lazarevic wrote an amendment which is in Exhibit P1967 and that one was signed by him. We say looking at these documents you follow the chain from that directive that issued from the very stop, the Supreme Command Staff or at that time the General Staff of the VJ from General Ojdanic. It goes through Pavkovic who issues his own Grom 3, orders Lazarevic to prepare an order to implement that, and you have Lazarevic's order in P2808, and it eventually gets implemented in joint VJ and MUP actions on the ground by the likes of Colonel Gergar and Colonel Zivaljevic or by Delic, Vukovic, and Mitrovic in late March 1999, and those actions link up to the crime sites and the crimes alleged in the indictment. As I said, further evidence of that is found in Exhibits P2015, P1981, and P1995. And if I may, I would like to direct you to some points in connection with each of those documents. P2015 is a Joint Command order number 455-63, dated the 23rd of March, 1999, directing the subordinate VJ units to provide assistance to the MUP in destroying Siptar terrorists in Orahovac, Suva Reka and Velika Krusa. The 549the Brigade in joint action with the MUP is to carry out an attack from Bela Crkva, et cetera, and destroy the Siptar terrorists in Celina, Mala Krusa, Pirane, et cetera, all sites which are named in our indictment and from which we've heard evidence about. And the order also says the Joint Command shall command those actions. P1981 is Colonel Delic's order pursuant to that Joint Command order in P2015. It is dated the 23rd of March, 1999, and General Delic orders that his Battle Group 1 is given a task in item 5.4 of that order. In cooperation with one company of the 37th PJP detachment and two platoons of the MUP energetically attack, overpower and destroy the Siptar terrorists in Mala Krusa, destroy the Siptar terrorists in the village of Pirane. Battle Group 2 of the 549th in cooperation with the 4th Company of the PJP is to "carry out an energetic attack and search Bela Crkva, come out on a certain line and then "destroy the Siptar terrorists in the village of Celine and the village of Nogavac." Again, this is dated the 23rd of March. Readiness to start that action was to be at 0700 hours on the 25th of March, 1999. And we say, Your Honour, that activity, that order matches up precisely with the crimes alleged in our indictment in that area and as testified to by villagers from those crime sites. But that's not the end. We have General -- or then Colonel Delic's post-action analysis regarding that order which is found in Exhibit P1995. That's dated the 30th of March, 1999. It's entitled submission of the analysis of the operation of the 549th Motorised Brigade in routing of the Siptar terrorists in the general area of Rotimlje and lifting the blockade on the Suva Reka-Orahovac road. He tells us in the period from the 25th of March until the 29th of March, 1999, pursuant to the order by the commander of the 549th and pursuant to the order by the Pristina Corps, strictly confidential number 455-63, which is Exhibit P2015, the Siptar terrorists were routed from that general area and full control has been established in the territory from the Prizren-Zrze road up to the Suva Reka-Orahovac road. Now, I'd like to show you an excerpt and then give you a graphic representation of what that looked like. You should see on the screen now that excerpt that I just read and if we could go to a map. This is from the Kosovo atlas showing that area, and we will move in in our next photograph. You will see on the lower left we've now highlighted in sort of bright pink the Prizren-Zrze road, and the Suva Reka-Orahovac road to show the outer borders of this area that Colonel Delic tells us they have now established full control over in the course of these actions. And if we could go to the next slide. We've drawn a border on the remaining two edges that are consistent with the road from Zrze to Orahovac and from Pristina to Suva Reka to show you the area that that appears to be describing as being under the full control. And one more slide, please. We've now indicated various locations named in the indictment where crimes occurred, Bela Crkva, Nogavac, Celina, Mala Krusa, Pirane, and Landovica. All these in the areas where the operations were carried out by the VJ and Colonel Delic in supporting the MUP. And in that post-action analysis I need to indicate a number of other things to you. Colonel Delic told us that involved there were some 2.020 men, I think about 1.000 MUP and 1.000 VJ, some 21 tanks, six 122-millimetre howitzers, and you'll see in the report itself other armoured vehicles and heavy weapons. Colonel Delic told us that the operation or the task was "completed successfully" and that the commanding was "under the Joint Command of the MUP and the VJ." One other interesting note I'd like to bring your attention to because I did discuss this with General Delic when he was here, not only in relation, I think, to this specific action but to a couple of others earlier in March before the war started. Page 2 of Exhibit P1995. He estimates that about 85 Siptar terrorists were killed and there were no prisoners. I think on operations described in Exhibits P1998 and 1999 you will also see that a number of terrorists were killed but no prisoners were taken by the 549th in joint actions with the MUP. Now, above that reference, Colonel Delic makes reference to the Siptar terrorists. He says "During the operation the Siptar terrorists did not throw their weapons and combat equipment before the crucial moment. When they started changing into civilian clothes and attempted to make a breakthrough along a certain trig point where they encountered our units in the line of blockade." But then there's no further details about what happened to them. Siptar terrorists were killed. There were no prisoners taken. Some of them threw down their weapons and changed into civilian clothes, tried to break out but failed to do so because they ran into the blockade, but then there is nothing indicating about what happened to them when they ran into the blockade and there's no indication prisoners were taken. We would ask you to examine that evidence closely and read it in conjunction with the testimony of the crime base victims from Bela Crkva, Nogavac, Celina, Mala Krusa, et cetera. Now, I'd like to look at another directive from General Ojdanic. This is P1481 dated the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just one -- do you relate all of this so far to the Grom 3 directive?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now I'm on to another topic and a different directive. This is P1481, 9th of April. You'll recall that there was one meeting of the VJ collegium during the war that we have minutes for and that was on the 9th of April. We say this directive came out of that meeting or was done during that meeting, in the course of that meeting. This is a directive "for engagement of the VJ in defence against the NATO aggression." And in that directive the engagement of the VJ up to that point in time is discussed. At page 4 in the English at the top it notes that the VJ realise the following task before the NATO aggression began. Increased security on the state borders, combat operations to block and destroy the Siptar terrorists forces in Kosovo and Metohija and mobilisation of war units in the preparation for combat use. This directive talks about the general aim of the defence. One of the tasks to be completed is to smash and destroy the Siptar terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija. The 3rd Army is given the task to smash and destroy the Siptar terrorists and prevent their withdrawal into the zone of the 2nd Army. At page 9 in the English it's indicated that in addition to VJ units "engage work obligation units and the -- and the organised population (volunteers) for maintenance of forthcoming and dummy positions." And one item of interest to us here related to other matters in this directive is item number 6 on page 11, command and communications. It talks about deployment of the Supreme Defence Council and the VJ General Staff. And it also talks about communications and cryptographic protections "at the level of VSO, Supreme Defence Council, and VJ General Staff, organised communication and cryptographic protection of information with president of the Republic of Serbia and president of the Republic of Montenegro, et cetera." So as of April 9th, in this directive General Ojdanic is providing for communications and making reference to deployment of the Supreme Defence Council. Now, we don't have a record -- we don't have a document entitled Supreme Defence Council Meeting in 1999 after the war started, but we've had this discussion about the evidence regarding a Supreme Command and who was on the Supreme Command. I'll talk about that some more in a minute but I want to continue on about this directive. After that directive was issued on the 9th of April -- or the same day, I should say, General Ojdanic issued what was titled a preparatory order to General Pavkovic. It's Exhibit P1480. And he tells him to obey the directive tasking you with preparing a proposal for dealing with the aggression by the Siptar terrorists forces and aggression by NATO. That proposal was to be submitted to the Supreme Command by 2000 hours on the 10th of April and then there was to be a report on the proposal for a decision on the 11th of April at the Supreme Command Staff in the presence of the Supreme Commander. This is further verified by Exhibit 3D815 dated the 10th of April, 1999, which is a combat report of the Supreme Command Staff. Item number 7 on page 8 says a directive for the further use of the Yugoslav army has been produced at the level of the Supreme Command Staff. The directive was immediately sent to the 3rd Army command for the preparation and briefing on a decision of the 3rd Army command. And following up from that we see on the 10th of April, 1999, from General Pavkovic as commander of the 3rd Army a document that is titled Grom 4. It's entitled order for engagement of the 3rd Army in defence from NATO aggression. And it's similar in style and content and format to what we saw in Grom 3 from General Pavkovic. There's one puzzling note related to this. As I said, you saw that directive on the 9th of April from the Supreme Command Staff and the order, the preparatory order to General Pavkovic and his ground for Grom 4 on the 10th of April, but we have in evidence in Exhibit 5D175 an order of the Pristina Corps related to Grom 4. It's confidential number 455-123. So it's in that series with the Joint Command orders. However, it's dated the 6th of April, three days before the directive from the Supreme Command Staff, four days before General Pavkovic issues his Grom 4. I looked at the original to make sure that date was correct. It does appear to be. It's hard to know how General Lazarevic knew about Grom 4 before the directive was issued and before General Pavkovic issued his Grom 4, but I only advise the Court of that for you to make of it what -- what you can and what you will. I tried to see if there was anything further to suggest that perhaps there was an error. I know that the date on my English translation says 6 April 1998, but I believe on the original it is 1999, and other evidence within the document makes it clear that it is April 1999. You know, we have in evidence a logbook of all the 455 series documents, and 455-123 is listed in the logbook as being on the 4th of April, 1999. I know that probably only adds to the confusion, but I raise this point because one of the things General Lazarevic told you when he testified -- when he received a directive from Pavkovic like Grom 3 and he issued his Grom 3 order in P2808, I asked him about well, why did you put in this stuff about engaging the armed non-Siptar population, and he said well, I have to do that because that comes from my commander and that's a part I can't change, I have to leave that the same. But in this one, 5D175, which is apparently issued by Lazarevic three, four, six days before General Pavkovic's Grom 4, in this order under the task for the Pristina Corps, item number 2 on page 3, he says use armed non-Siptar population to secure military features and features of special importance for the defence of FRY, the roads, and for the defence of populated areas. I bring that to your attention because later on in connection with General Lazarevic I'll be arguing about issues of credibility. Now, I'm still continuing on about this 9 April directive. On the 11th of April we have one of the evening briefings of the Supreme Command Staff, and at page 3 of that evening briefing, this is Exhibit 3D728, General Ojdanic is talking about the directive and he says: "During the evening amended the directive in line with ours. Submit the draft plan for study. The briefing will be at 0900 with the VK." And you will remember we had some discussion about what that acronym or what that abbreviation means, whether it means Supreme Commander or Supreme Command. There was some debate. We had one witness who said oh, no, no, Supreme Command would always be a "BK" and a little "a." But I think Mr. Zecevic himself and General Gajic, Branko Gajic, told us actually "BK" could be either one, could be Supreme Commander or could be Supreme Command depending on the context. And that reference is found at page 15415 where both Mr. Zecevic and General Gajic tell you that it could be -- could stand for either. I say in the context of this meeting it is referring to the Supreme Command, because the very next thing it says in that document at page 3 is present -- this is apparently a list of people who will be at that meeting the next day. Present the deputy for operations and staff affairs, the Chief of Operations administration, the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff, General Smiljanic, General Grga, President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, and Sreten, adjutant of the MUP unit from Kosovo who we have to assume must be Sreten Lukic. And the English translation I had says 2nd Lieutenant Sainovic, but I think we got it resolved later on that acronym in the B/C/S really stands for vice-president and not 2nd lieutenant, Sainovic and General Pavkovic. So that to be discussed at a meeting the next day, and the next information we have concerning that original directive on the 9th of April is dated the 12th of April, 1999. This is Exhibit P1483. It's from the Supreme Command Staff signed by General Ojdanic. It's titled supplement to directive DT number 22-1 of 9 April 1999 that makes some changes. One change that we think is important for you to take note of on page 2 says paragraph 6 of the original directive should be changed to read "forces of the MUP and civilian defence shall be placed under the command of the 3rd Army during the operation and they shall be used exclusively by your decision." So General Ojdanic on the 9th of April is purporting to put the forces of the MUP and the civilian defence under the command of General Pavkovic for those -- those actions, that operation. One more directive I want to talk about just briefly is P1465. It's from the Supreme Command Staff. It's dated the 29th of May, 1999, and it's a warning or a reminder depending on which translation you look at, and the point I wanted to make about this is the first paragraph. It notes that: "The intensive engagement of the Pristina Corps units in smashing Siptar terrorist forces prevented their maximum engagement in preparations to counter a NATO land operation." The point I'm trying to make is that General Ojdanic is clearly aware that prior to the 29th of May, 1999, rather than engaging and preparing to counter a NATO land attack, the VJ forces have been intensively engaged, the Pristina Corps, intensively engaged in smashing the Siptar terrorist forces. Now, that's from the Supreme Command Staff, and it's echoed or reflected in a 3rd Army command order the following day, 30 May 1999, which is P1614 from General Pavkovic to the Pristina Corps. General Lazarevic says the intensive engagement of your units in smashing Siptar terrorist forces prevented their maximum engagement in preparations to counter this NATO operation. Now, the second way in which we say General Ojdanic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise was in relation to arming of the non-Siptars. You will recall that there were a few references to arming the non-Siptars and the number of armed Serbs in Kosovo and some of the VJ collegiums. One of the first references was in P928, a meeting on the 30th of December, 1998, where I believe it was General Dimitrijevic was talking about the situation in Kosovo, and at page 9 of the English of that exhibit he says: "I'm thinking of a figure of about 60.000 armed Serbs that can be mobilised outside the control of the official organs." On the 21st of January, 1999, that's Exhibit P939, again General Dimitrijevic in his report is saying at page 16 of the English: "On the other hand, bearing in mind the number of people owning or having been distributed weapons there is a realistic possibility on the Serbian and Montenegrin side of the Serbian population organising itself to offer resistance and of an increasing emergence of radical forces." Again, this is a meeting of the VJ collegium presided over by General Ojdanic as the chief for the General Staff. And the most telling one, I think is in P931, the VJ collegium minutes for the 2nd of February, 1999. You will recall we talked about this one with a number of witnesses. Page 23 of the English, General Ojdanic says: "I've heard that there are 50.000 armed Serbs." General Samardzic, who is no longer commander of the 3rd Army but he's in that position as inspectorate of the VJ says: "Judging by the amount of weapons issued for now it's 47.000, by the amount of the weapons and rest assured that several thousand of them have already left with the weapons." Ojdanic says: "What are the war assignments of those armed Serbs and what is the plan for including them in the units?" And Samardzic says: "It was my order, and we organised the whole thing for the defence of Serbian villages. Commanders at all levels have been sent out. They're armed and they have two combat sets of ammunition each.
