Their role and assignment is to defend their villages and participate together with army units in any operations in the immediate vicinity. We have to carry out military and police operations. It can't be done in any other way and at this moment there are enough army and MUP units to do that part of the job if it should come to that." Now, he said, "It was my order," and we can see where that order was. If you will look at Exhibit P1415. This is a document dated 26th of June, 1998, about eight months earlier, and this is an order -- this particular document is an order from General Pavkovic as the commander of the Pristina Corps at that time, but it says: "Pursuant to the 3rd Army command, strictly confidential number such-and-such," so that would have been General Samardzic as commander of the 3rd Army at the time. And this calls for the distribution of weapons and ammunition with two combat sets of ammunition. It talks about on the basis of the list call up military conscripts and small groups to the army barracks or organise distribution and issue weapons in Serbian and Montenegrin villages. Devote special attention to security measures, secrecy and camouflage, discipline in carrying out the task. Item number 6 says: "After completing the distribution, prepare and organise inhabited places for defence. Military department commanders are responsible for organising this in their zones of responsibility in cooperation with the MUP and local self-government organs." So we've got the VJ, the MUP, the military department and the local government -- self-government organs all working together to do this. An active superior officer of the VJ is to be placed in charge of each settlement, and responsibility for these tasks in item number 9 on page 2, unit commanders are responsible for the distribution of weapons and military department commanders for forming and training of the units. So we say P1415 is the document that reflects the order that Samardzic says in February 1999 that he gave earlier. All right. Now -- and I'll talk more about that particular aspect when we come to General Pavkovic, but I want to move on to another way which we say General Ojdanic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise, and that was his role in the Supreme Defence Council and during the war time the Supreme Command. Although he was a non-voting member of the SDC, he made important personnel proposals. That was his job, and some of the proposals that he made after he became Chief of the General Staff and member of the SDC was a proposal regarding General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic and General Farkas. In the minutes of the 8th session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 25th of December, 1998, a meeting attended by the way by Mr. Sainovic as well, among the items on the agenda were the appointments, promotions, assignments of new duties of several generals, and this is a meeting where it was proposed that General Pavkovic be elevated to be commander of the 3rd Army and General Lazarevic to be commander of the 3rd Army Corps -- I mean of the Pristina Corps. I'm sorry. And you will recall we had a lot of -- we had a lot of evidence and discussion about this document, because this is the meeting where President Djukanovic expressed some reservations about the proposal to promote or to elevate General Pavkovic because of the conflicting information coming from Kosovo in recent months regarding the involvement of the Pristina Corps, the indication that the Pristina Corps' actions were not always in accordance with the constitutional role of the army and the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. You will remember that's the one where Mr. Milosevic sort of pooh-poohed Djukanovic's concerns and said no, no, no, there was nothing. There had been no complaints about any illegal action by the Pristina Corps, either from abroad or from any side, but Milutinovic to his credit, I say, was a little more honest. He added that some reports of the alleged lack of discipline and unconstitutional actions by the Pristina Corps were usually "inflated." Now, General Ojdanic is at this meeting. He's made the proposal. He hears the complaints. Keep that in mind because one of the things we will argue later on is that General Ojdanic was on notice about some problems with General Pavkovic and we say that he failed to take appropriate actions in that regard and this is something I want you to keep in mind when we get to that discussion. Further with regard to his role in the Supreme Command, during the war Ojdanic met regularly with the Supreme Command for instructions which he converted to tasks for the VJ. You've heard evidence about that. There's more detail in our brief on that point. One other item that relates to that relationship is Exhibit P1010. This is a Politika article. It's an interview of General Ojdanic on the 29th of April, 1999. The article's about the high morale of the Yugoslav army, and on page 3 of the English the next to the last paragraph General Ojdanic says: "I am sure that in future we shall execute tasks given to us by the Supreme Command led by President Slobodan Milosevic as we have until now, successfully." We say another bit of evidence indicating the existence of a Supreme Command being something greater than just Mr. Milosevic as the Supreme Commander during the wartime. Another way in which we say General Ojdanic contributed to the joint criminal enterprise was related to the October agreements. We say General Ojdanic was aware of certain VJ violations of those agreements including the bringing in to Kosovo of additional forces, the non-return of heavy equipment loaned to the MUP and some other matters detailed in our brief. Just quickly one of those is in Exhibit P941, VJ collegium minutes for the 25th of February, 1999. You will recall General Dimitrijevic talking in that meeting about the anti-terrorist battalion from the 72nd Special Brigade having been dispatched apparently initially to the rim of Kosovo and then into Kosovo. General Ojdanic noted on page 16 of the English of that meeting that the essence of the matter was not to bring that unit to Kosovo. So again here's another example of where he's aware of something that General Pavkovic has done that should cause him some concern and perhaps require him to take some action. Another violation we say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: With the leave of the Presiding Judge, if I might, in respect of the October agreement and alleged breaches. Would the October agreement have been based on any premise as to the conduct of the KLA or the Albanians and how they would or would not act in the circumstances given the obligations under the October agreements? And I'm interested to hear from you whether there would have been any legitimate or reasonable expectations as to their conduct under the October agreements and how this would affect your arguments thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a -- that's a difficult issue. The KLA was not a signatory to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I -- even given that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To me it presents a bizarre circumstance that they aren't included in the situation. I know -- I think we heard Shaun Byrnes testify to that somewhat, to some extent that they -- that he in KDOM and some of the other internationals tried to use their good -- their good services to the best of their ability to persuade KLA perhaps not to move back into this area and not be aggressive but they had no -- they had no force behind that other than, you know, to try and persuade them by reason or perhaps suggesting that if you -- if you continue to act this way you may not get what you want. In the end you may not have our support, et cetera. But there wasn't any enforcement mechanism. There wasn't anything in the agreement to make them act that way. Now, I don't know. I guess if you were going to argue on the basis of contract law, you would come down in one position but in real life I don't know. It seems to me looking now with the advantage of 20/20 hindsight saying that was -- that was an enterprise doomed to failure. If there wasn't some mechanism in place to be able to control the KLA, it seems that it was ill-advised to go forward with the agreement, but I don't know that I've answered your question, Judge. It's just a difficult matter for me to accept, but it seems clear to me that the Yugoslav side was aware of that when they entered into the agreement. Now, whether or not they had any realistic option, that's a matter beyond me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to thank you for that answer, and I -- there is another matter that would concern me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In the event of provocation or circumstances where it would be believed that it was necessary to respond, how does the OTP say that the -- the forces should have responded under the terms of the agreement? I'd like that to be set out and laid out for me a bit more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My understanding from the evidence is that everyone sort of understood that in the event that there was a provocation by the KLA, if the KLA attacked the police or -- or the VJ, that they were entitled to respond to that attack, defend themselves and respond with appropriate force, but as to the particulars of what that meant in a particular situation I think different parties may have had different views, but I think everyone agreed that yes, they did have that right. Part of what we've argued about in this case, though, is that sometimes what was being recorded as a provocation, I guess it has more to do with timing, because as I understand it, that agreement was well, if we're marching down the road and we're attacked by KLA, we're certainly entitled to defend ourselves. And if we chase them into the hills and kill them, we're entitled to do that, too, if it's in immediate response. But I think what we see happening sometimes is that there may have been an attack on the MUP or the VJ last week and this week, seven days or ten days later, the VJ and MUP get organised and we're going to go to that village where we think those guys came from and then we're going to respond. And I think that's where some of us argue that no, that wasn't -- it's too late now, that's not -- that's not a response; that's an initiative on your own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you, Judge. Thank you. The next reference to what we say was a violation of the October agreements mentioned in the VJ collegiums was on the 3rd of December, 1998. That's in Exhibit 3D557, page 19. General Obradovic is talking about certain equipment that the VJ had loaned to the MUP, in particular this related to 20 personnel carriers. I believe those were armed personnel carriers, APCs, and 23 mortars that were subject to the OSCE agreement. And they were talking about, well, should we list this equipment as being with us and the VJ? But then if they inspect, they may discover that no, we don't really have it, that the MUP has it. Or we could list it as being with the MUP, but then we need to have some documentation about how it was handed over. And then there's also mention about problems with two helicopters that the Serbian MUP has acquired, whether that should be presented as being part of the army or being presented as being the MUP. It appears that the VJ collegium was of two minds about how to do this. General Dimitrijevic weighed in and made a comment. He said, "I'm against presenting falsely in our documents that they're with us, but I think this has to be done at the highest level. The equipment should be returned, but if we're going to keep it we should present it as MUP equipment and then let them introduce a convention," whatever that means. It's the same with the helicopters and it's not two helicopters; there are more. Ojdanic says, "I will first try with the minister," and I think in this context that means Minister Stojiljkovic, "and after that I must seek FRY president's position. I also am not for either one or the other because the inspection team will come. The same thing goes for the helicopters because in those talks with the foreign military representatives among other things they ask us about helicopter gunships and their firing observed on such-and-such a day in such-and-such a place and at such-and-such a feature. So those are two issues to be briefly described and I'll inform the president." So Ojdanic didn't seem to be necessarily opposed to taking ab action that would falsely represent to the OSCE what the position was regarding that particular heavy equipment. Now, the last item in connection with our argument about contributions to the JCE is -- is -- is a bit unusual to me in a way conceptually. We talk about failings regarding Pavkovic and it's detailed in our brief and we say General Ojdanic had good cause to believe that Pavkovic was not fully and accurately reporting about VJ activities in Kosovo and that General Ojdanic was also aware that General Pavkovic was dealing occasionally directly with President Milosevic without informing Ojdanic either before or after the fact. This is detailed in the brief in paragraph 757 through 766 of our final brief. You will recall some of the discussions with witnesses including General Dimitrijevic about discussions at the VJ collegium. I think the earliest one was probably in July 1998 when General Pavkovic was still commander of the Pristina Corps, and there was -- General Perisic was expressing a concern that his ban on the use of VJ units in Kosovo without his specific permission was being violated by someone and we say the best evidence suggested at that time that was General Pavkovic. So -- and this went on for months, and there were at least, I think, three other occasions where this is discussed. It's usually General Dimitrijevic bringing it up. General Ojdanic acknowledges that there's a problem on at least one occasion. He says there's obviously something not right here and we need to have General Pavkovic come in and talk to him, but there's no evidence that that happened or that was done. Now, I'll talk some more about that tomorrow, I guess, when we get to General Pavkovic, but we say with this clear knowledge that there's not full reporting and that sometimes the person who is not reporting is taking actions that are contrary to instructions and contrary to the October agreements and later on not taking any action is in effect a tacit approval by General Ojdanic of what Pavkovic has done. As I said, we'll talk more about that tomorrow. Shared intent. We say General Ojdanic shared the intent in connection with the joint criminal enterprise because he had a wealth of knowledge about crimes being committed by the forces of FRY and Serbia in Kosovo in both 1998 and 1999, yet he continued to participate in planning and ordering combat actions that led to further crimes by those same forces. This, too, Your Honour, is set forth in further detail in our final brief in paragraphs 783 to 807. We say that General Ojdanic's awareness of the allegations of prior crimes and the misuse of the Pristina Corps in 1998 combined with the well-known international complaints in 1999 and problems with reporting by Pavkovic personally known to General Ojdanic called for more robust measures to be taken than the ones that he did. In addition, there are VJ statistics regarding crimes which support the inference that the measures that he did take were -- were too little and too late and they were not adequate. I don't -- I don't think I have the time, Your Honours, to go through some of the exhibits I would like to, but you will recall that in connection with the military courts and proceedings in the military court we've had a number of exhibits. I would refer you to P953, P954, P955 which I think were brought in by General Gojevic, and P962 which is General -- or Colonel Delic's report on measures taken against members of the 549th Brigade, and P1011 which is that report by Mr. Markovic, not Professor Markovic but a different Markovic, on how the VJ complied with international law all have a number of statistics about the number of cases, but if you read them closely and you review the evidence and the cross-examination of those witnesses, you see there are a number of inconsistencies that should cause you some pause or some concern about how -- how effective these courts and prosecutors were, if that was a result of the difficulties of trying to do cases in the war or if it was also partly a result of a -- a lack of desire to really pursue that. The overwhelming majority of those prosecutions, you had high numbers thrown at you that we prosecuted this many thousand violations, but I think if you look statistics, 90 per cent of those are crimes against the VJ like failure to respond to the call-up and going Awol and insubordination to your superior officer. The crimes like our crimes, murder, rape, looting, robbery, are a very, very small percentage, and the percentage of those where the perpetrator is a Serb and the victim is a non-Serb is even much smaller. So we urge you to have a look at that evidence as well. Your Honours, I know we're about five minutes from the time but I'm about to go into General Pavkovic and I wonder if we could recess a few minutes early today.
